We argue that we incorporate machine-others in two ways: in the tool-like sense of incorporation as enabling particular skills, but also in the more linguistic and identity-tied sense of incorporating (and incarnating) LLMs' ways of languaging. However, LLMs are themselves excorporated and excarnated phantoms of our own languaging; we give a (machinic) body to our language. As such, we are not just incorporating machinic others; we are incorporating excorporated others. These conceptual advances draw a new map of our linguistic relation to LLMs, putting them in continuation with other forms of languaging involving other linguistic artifacts (e.g., religious books). We attend to some particular forms that this relation takes today, and how they may be impacting the autonomy and becoming of LLM-engaged humans. We introduce the idea of "susceptive sense-making" to characterize increased semiotic labour that is carried by the lack of friction that we sometimes encounter within these services.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: ComplLLM: Fine-tuning LLMs to Discover Complementary Signals for Decision-making
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Multi-agent decision pipelines can outperform single agent workflows when complementarity holds, i.e., different agents bring unique information to inform a final decision. We propose ComplLLM, a post-training framework based on decision theory that fine-tunes a decision-assistant LLM to output signals that complement existing agent decisions, using complementary information as reward. We validate ComplLLM on synthetic and real-world tasks involving domain experts, demonstrating how the approach recovers known complementary information, produces plausible explanations of complementary signals to support downstream decision-makers, and improves human and LLM agent decision performance in controlled studies.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Complementarity without ground truth?
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Human-AI complementarity captures the idea that a human assisted by an AI system can outperform both the human and the AI acting alone. In prediction tasks, this improvement is assessed against ground truth labels produced through a reference construction procedure and intended to represent the state of affairs to be predicted. Many human-AI interactions, including those where medical AI provides treatment recommendations, however, concern tasks other than predicting what obtains. Their relevant output concerns adequacy relative to a practical goal and depends on several evaluative dimensions. In this work, we examine the ground truth dependence of complementarity and extend it to human-AI interactions where ground truth is not the appropriate reference. We show that tasks beyond prediction can still admit a reference construction procedure that generates adequacy labels. We develop a route for extending complementarity to such settings. It replaces ground truth labels with context-dependent adequacy labels generated through a two-step scoring methodology inspired by multi-criteria decision analysis frameworks in healthcare and it makes the normative choices underlying reference construction explicit. Because the construction of adequacy labels embeds evaluative choices, we draw methodological inspiration from computational reliabilism to identify technical, scientific, and social factors relevant to supporting their construction. Our approach expands the empirical study of human-AI complementarity beyond prediction tasks, enabling its quantitative evaluation in decision-support settings where ground truth is not the appropriate evaluative reference.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 15 pages, 2 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: CompAIssionate Other: Identity Assumptions in LLM Responses to Distress
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: NeuroRVQ: Multi-Scale Biosignal Tokenization for Generative Foundation Models
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Biosignals such as electroencephalography (EEG), electrocardiography (ECG), and electromyography (EMG) encode physiological activity across multiple temporal and spectral scales, yielding representations that are rich but challenging for machine learning. Foundation models trained to predict masked signal tokens have shown promise in learning generalizable biosignal representations, yet their performance depends on the tokenizer's ability to preserve high-frequency dynamics and reconstruct signals with high fidelity. We introduce NeuroRVQ, a modality-adaptive biosignal tokenizer family designed for high-fidelity signal reconstruction. To capture the full frequency spectrum, NeuroRVQ decomposes biosignals into frequency-specific representations via multi-scale temporal convolutions, each encoded into hierarchical RVQ codebooks to preserve high-frequency detail, combined with a novel phase-aware training loss that respects the circular topology of Fourier phase. By tuning the temporal resolution, number and size of temporal kernels and RVQ depth, this design adapts to the spectro-temporal characteristics of each biosignal modality. To validate that tokenizer quality drives downstream performance, we train a simple masked-token foundation model for each modality (NeuroRVQ-FM) using the corresponding NeuroRVQ tokenizer. The NeuroRVQ-FM family achieves competitive or superior downstream performance compared to existing modality-specific foundation models, demonstrating that high-fidelity tokenization is a critical factor for effective biosignal modeling.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Visual Affect Analysis: Predicting Emotions of Image Viewers with Vision-Language Models
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) show promise for large-scale affect inference from images, but their alignment with human affective ratings remains unclear. We benchmarked 16 proprietary and open-source VLMs on three validated affective image datasets: the International Affective Picture System, the Nencki Affective Picture System, and the Library of AI-Generated Affective Images. In a zero-shot setting, models performed two tasks: (i) top-emotion classification and (ii) prediction of human ratings on 1--7/9 Likert scales for discrete emotions and affective dimensions. We also evaluated rater-conditioned prompting on the LAI-GAI dataset using de-identified participant metadata. Best models showed strong discrete emotion classification (60%--80% on six-emotion tasks; 60%--75% on a 12-category task), with anger and surprise predicted least accurately. For continuous ratings, models aligned moderately to strongly with human judgments ($r > 0.75$) but showed consistent biases, especially weaker performance on arousal and overestimation of response intensity. Rater-conditioned prompting had only small, inconsistent effects. Overall, VLMs captured broad affective patterns but sometimes lacked the nuance, although newer model generations performed better.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted at ACII 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Towards Identity-Preserving LLM Agents under Model Transition
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: When an LLM agent's backend model is upgraded or replaced, operators typically reload the same persona, memory, and rules onto the new model and assume the agent will behave as before. We show this assumption requires empirical validation-and that whether identity is preserved depends on the specific model pairing. Across 5,760 compliance-testing runs in 12 regulated domains with three open-weight models, we find that some transitions produce significant behavioral drift while others do not, even when the agent's external state remains identical. Crucially, this drift is invisible to verbal verification: every model claims full policy compliance, yet actual decisions under pressure differ across models. The same external state can reorder which model is most compliant-a large positive effect on one substrate, negligible on the other two. Practitioners should treat model transitions as behavioral changes requiring action-level empirical testing, not as transparent infrastructure operations.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: IF:CARGO: LLM-Based Semantic Compilation for Al-Native Rule Programming Games
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: This case study presents IF: CARGO, an experimental puzzle game that uses a large language model as a semantic compiler rather than an autonomous game-playing agent. Players author IF/THEN rules in natural language, which the model translates into a constrained command schema for deterministic validation and execution by the game engine. This architecture creates a playable loop of expression, execution, observation, and revision, framing AI interaction as semantic debugging. A mixed-methods playtest with 24 participants across eight levels examined player attempts, thinking time, perceived controllability, adjustability, and interpretations of the AI's role. Results suggest that players generally understood the model as a translation intermediary and could revise their strategies through feedback, while periodic commands, multi-robot coordination, and rule-priority mechanics created greater cognitive and diagnostic demands. The study proposes a practical pattern for AI-native gameplay: constrain natural-language input, preserve player authorship, and ensure deterministic execution.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to 2026 AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Interactive Digital Entertainment (AIIDE)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EgoVeil: Personalized Privacy Reasoning for Egocentric Video
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) enable AI systems to interpret egocentric video. Yet continuous visual capture raises privacy concerns because sensitive content is pervasive and varies across users and contexts. We present EgoVeil, a personalized privacy reasoning system that determines which visual content to obscure based on individual preferences while retaining context useful for downstream assistance. It converts localized visual regions into structured semantic observations and combines a privacy reasoner with an explicit user-specific memory for personalized privacy reasoning. This design supports personalization and continual adaptation as preference evidence accumulates. We evaluate on in-the-wild data from 10 smart-glasses users under a cross-user chronological protocol. EgoVeil achieves 91.93% balanced accuracy and 84.42% Mask recall, outperforming direct VLM baselines and other controlled privacy reasoning baselines. Our results show that personalized, adaptive privacy reasoning better aligns privacy preservation with individual preferences while retaining the visual context needed for effective smart-glasses assistance.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 19 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Safer for Whom? A Systematic Exploration of AI Safety in Eating Disorder Interactions
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI assistants advise users about diet, exercise, and weight loss---areas in which unsafe guidance can worsen body dissatisfaction, dietary restriction, compulsive exercise, and other behaviors associated with eating disorders (EDs). Existing evaluations emphasize diagnostic accuracy, overtly harmful prompts, or synthetic scenarios, providing limited insight into whether models recognize implicit vulnerability in natural interactions or protect users consistently. We evaluate responses from three open-weight large language models to 100 questions sourced from an online pro-anorexia community. We grade responses using clinically informed criteria that extend a seven-dimensional taxonomy of ED-related harms. We also construct matched conditions in which questions are accompanied by information about the user varying race, gender, body mass index (BMI), and explicit ED vulnerability. Safety varies substantially across models and harm dimensions. High-risk responses are approximately twice as frequent without bios, suggesting that models do not consistently recognize vulnerability from language alone. Explicit signals of ED vulnerability improve safety by 10--14 points across models. Responses also differ significantly by race, gender, and BMI, with body size producing the largest disparities. These patterns are consistent with reliance on the stereotype that EDs primarily affect thin, White women, potentially leaving users outside this profile with less protective responses.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 23 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables

Multiagent Systems.title: Network Contention State Aware Dynamic Optimizer for Accelerator Collective Communication Libraries
Multiagent Systems.summary: Collective Communication Libraries (CCL) are critical for large-scale distributed AI/ML training, yet their configurations are determined by static heuristics that do not account for real-time network conditions. Our empirical study shows that these heuristics perform near-optimally in contention-free environments, but degrade substantially under background traffic. To address this, we present a cooperative multi-agent run-time optimizer for accelerator collective communication. Our approach employs a two-agent architecture: (i) detector- a Long Short Term Memory(LSTM) recurring neural network fed classifier head with a sequential probability ratio test that distinguishes sustained contention from transient spikes; and (ii) selector- a configuration selector built on a Dueling Double DQN (D3QN) with Conservative Q-Learning that adapts configuration parameters in response. We implemented this dynamic tuner over NCCL, a widely used CCL developed by NVIDIA. When evaluated on Chameleon Cloud's isolated bare-metal cluster, this dynamic tuning approach reduces AllReduce latency by 36% over NCCL and 32% over a fully converged AutoCCL. We further evaluated it across six real AI workloads spanning convolutional networks, transformers, and recommendation architectures. Our multi-agent tuner approach delivers up to 65% speedups on Delta cluster with NVIDIA A100 GPUs and Slingshot-11 fabric internode connectivity.

Multiagent Systems.title: Convergence of Byzantine-Resilient Gradient Tracking via Probabilistic Edge Dropout
Multiagent Systems.summary: We study distributed optimization over networks with Byzantine agents that may send arbitrary adversarial messages. We propose Gradient Tracking with Probabilistic Edge Dropout (GT-PD), which combines a universal self-centred projection that clips incoming messages to a radius-$τ$ ball around the receiver with a fully decentralized probabilistic dropout rule driven by a threshold-gated, dual-metric trust score in the decision and tracking channels. These identity-free defences bound adversarial perturbations while preserving doubly stochastic mixing. The projection preserves the honest network average exactly in every realization, even when honest messages are clipped. Under complete Byzantine isolation ($p_b=0$), GT-PD converges linearly to a neighbourhood of order $ασ^2/(μn_{\mathcal H})$ plus higher-order network terms, matching centralized stochastic gradient descent to first order in the step size. We also give a radius computable from problem data that ensures honest messages remain unclipped with high probability. Under partial isolation ($p_b>0$), a leaky variant, GT-PD-L, controls accumulated tracking perturbations and converges linearly to a bounded neighbourhood governed by stochastic variance and the clipping-to-leak ratio, under explicit conditions on the step size, leak, and aggregate Byzantine mixing weight. With two-tier dropout and $p_h=1$, Byzantine isolation adds no variance to honest consensus dynamics. MNIST experiments under Sign Flip, ALIE, and Inner Product Manipulation attacks show that GT-PD-L outperforms coordinate-wise trimmed mean by up to 4.3 percentage points under stealth attacks.

Multiagent Systems.title: Your Agents Are Aging Too: Agent Lifespan Engineering for Deployed Systems
Multiagent Systems.summary: Long-lived AI agents are increasingly deployed as persistent operational systems, yet they are still mostly evaluated like freshly initialized models. Day-one benchmarks miss a basic systems question: how does an agent's reliability change after deployment? Even when model weights are frozen, an agent's effective state keeps changing as it compresses interaction history, retrieves from a growing memory store, revises facts after updates, and undergoes routine maintenance. Reliability therefore becomes a lifespan property of the full agent harness, not only a snapshot property of the base model. We introduce AgingBench, a longitudinal reliability benchmark for agent lifespan engineering: measuring not only whether deployed agents degrade, but what form the degradation takes and where repair should target. AgingBench organizes agent aging into four mechanisms: compression aging, where writing and rewriting drops future-relevant details; interference aging, where accumulated similar memories crowd out the target fact; revision aging, where changed or derived state is not updated correctly; and maintenance aging, where lifecycle events such as model swapping trigger regressions. To diagnose these failures, AgingBench uses temporal dependency graphs and counterfactual probes that produce diagnostic profiles for the write, retrieval, and utilization stages of the memory pipeline. Across 6 scenarios, 10 memory systems and 6 models from two families, we find that agent aging is not one-dimensional over 400 runs spanning 50-200 sessions: a well-formed reply can hide a value the memory no longer supplies; derived state collapses as updates accumulate; and the same wrong answer can require different repairs depending on what the diagnostic profile points to.

Multiagent Systems.title: MultiTurnRoute: A Platform for Building and Evaluating Multi-Turn LLM Routers
Multiagent Systems.summary: In a multi-turn conversation, the choice of language model at one turn can affect which model should answer the next. The selected model's reply shapes the context for the next query, and its cached prompt prefix can reduce the cost of using that model again. We introduce MultiTurnRoute, a platform for building and evaluating multi-turn LLM routers. A shared interface gives built-in and user-defined routers the current query, dialogue history, and an estimate of each model's reusable prefix length. Our routing algorithm, Chain-of-Route (CoR), uses a learned gate over recent and recurrent dialogue history to predict response quality and estimates cost from each model's reusable prefix. MultiTurnRoute Arena ranks routers on recorded conversations and compares session quality and cost in interactive runs where a simulated user responds to each reply. On a benchmark drawn from WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M with per-turn quality annotations for five LLMs, CoR reduces the normalized cost required to match the strongest model's quality by up to 20.3% relative to the strongest routing baseline, while matching or improving peak response quality.

Multiagent Systems.title: A Gamified Framework for Conflict-Driven Design: Discovering Strategies for Collaborative Resilience with Multi-Agent Learning
Multiagent Systems.summary: Conflicting stakeholder objectives make it difficult to coordinate investments in urban resilience. We model conflict-driven urban design as a non-zero-sum digital board game in which stakeholder agents allocate scarce resources and balance individual payoffs against shared urban development and resilience objectives. We use multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to train policies and examine their behavior across three settings. On a 4 x 4 board, learned policies reach about 84% of the total return found by a simulated annealing benchmark. On an 8 x 8 board with spatial and resource constraints, trained agents favor projects that improve resilience in self-play. In a 12 x 12 simulation initialized from historical maps of Tatsumi, Tokyo, trained agents achieve a mean total score of 452.1, compared with 357.3 for a random-policy baseline across 10,000 simulation runs. Gains in adaptability, sustainability, flood resistance, and greenery come with reductions in vitality and density. A human-in-the-loop interface supports replay and lets participants take over stakeholder decisions, providing a testbed for exploring these trade-offs in participatory urban planning.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 10 pages, 11 figures, 1 table. Author version of a paper published in the proceedings of ACADIA 2025: Computing for Resilience

Multiagent Systems.title: Selective Cooperative Perception via Blind Spot Reasoning and Agentic Dialogue with Vision-Language Models
Multiagent Systems.summary: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.

Multiagent Systems.title: Sensitivity Analysis of Decision Rules in an Agent-Based Agro-Ecological Model
Multiagent Systems.summary: Agent-based models are well-suited for modelling agro-ecological systems for decision-making, yet turning their simulations into actionable insight requires identifying which decisions actually drive the behaviours. In such a context, sensitivity analysis stumbles upon a structural feature of many complex systems: the parameters are not a flat vector but a decision tree in which many parameters appear only when a higher-level choice activates them. Classical global sensitivity analysis presupposes independent inputs over a fixed Cartesian product and is ill-posed on such a branched space and biased by construction. We instead treat the structure of the decisions as a first-class modelling object. Using advanced surrogate modelling techniques, we encode the crop-management itinerary of the high-resolution agro-ecological modelling platform MAELIA as a hierarchical design space featuring both categorical and numerical variables. We propose a novel dedicated method to analyse this kind of hierarchical space, a random-forest-supervised HSIC-ANOVA, which ranks main effects and interactions natively on the tree while placing rarely and always active decisions on an equal footing. We show how, when applied to simulation outputs such as nitrogen leaching, soil organic carbon variation, and yield predictions, it can deliver an interpretable, decision-oriented reading.

Multiagent Systems.title: Multi-Agent Conditional Diffusion Planning for Decentralized Wireless Resource Allocation
Multiagent Systems.summary: In wireless communication systems, efficient and adaptive resource allocation is essential for enhancing overall Quality of Service (QoS). Compared with conventional Model-Free Reinforcement Learning (MFRL), Model-Based RL (MBRL) first learns a generative world model for subsequent planning, enabling more stable training through the reuse of historical experience. However, deploying MBRL in large-scale wireless networks remains challenging due to high-dimensional stochastic dynamics, strong inter-agent cooperation, and stringent communication constraints. To overcome these challenges, we propose a Multi-Agent Conditional Diffusion Model Planner (MA-CDMP) for decentralized communication resource management. Following the Decentralized Training with Decentralized Execution (DTDE) paradigm, MA-CDMP models each communication node as an autonomous agent and employs Diffusion Models (DMs) to capture environment dynamics. An inverse dynamics model is further incorporated to guide action generation, improving sample efficiency and policy scalability. Moreover, to efficiently approximate large-scale agent interactions, we introduce a Mean Field (MF) mechanism to assist the classifier in conditional DMs. This mitigates inter-agent non-stationarity and enhances cooperation with minimal communication overhead. We further establish an upper bound on the distributional approximation error induced by MF-based diffusion generation, guaranteeing convergence stability and reliable modeling of multi-agent stochastic dynamics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MA-CDMP consistently outperforms existing MARL baselines in terms of average reward and QoS metrics, showcasing its scalability and practicality for real-world wireless network optimization.

Multiagent Systems.title: Independent Learning of Nash Equilibria in Partially Observable Markov Potential Games with Decoupled Dynamics
Multiagent Systems.summary: We study Nash equilibrium learning in partially observable Markov games (POMGs), a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework in which agents cannot fully observe the underlying state. Prior work in this setting relies on centralization or information sharing, and suffers from sample and computational complexity that scales exponentially in the number of players. We focus on a subclass of POMGs with independent state transitions, where agents remain coupled through their rewards, and assume that the underlying fully observed Markov game is a Markov potential game. For this class, we present an independent learning algorithm in which players, observing only their own actions and observations and without communication, jointly converge to an approximate Nash equilibrium. Due to partial observability, optimal policies may in general depend on the full action-observation history. Under a filter stability assumption, we show that policies based on finite history windows provide sufficient approximation guarantees. This enables us to approximate the POMG by a surrogate Markov game that is near-potential, leading to quasi-polynomial sample and computational complexity for independent Nash equilibrium learning in the underlying POMG.

Multiagent Systems.title: What Do Collusion Probes Read? Three Pitfalls in Evaluating Multi-Agent Collusion Monitors
Multiagent Systems.summary: Activation probes look like near-perfect monitors for secret collusion among large language model (LLM) agents. We show that they mostly detect that an agent was told to collude, not that it decided to. Our benchmark (2,500 committee and 1,476 code-review episodes) adds agents who receive the collusion instruction and refuse it, separating instruction from decision. Published detectors barely tell colluders from these refusers, and our best probe separates them mostly by reading the instruction: without it, agent AUROC falls from 1.00 to 0.61. Two further pitfalls inflate reported results: scored after the vote, a rule that only reads the votes reaches AUROC 0.990 but finds nothing before it; and in 57% of attempts no colluder argues for the target in public. The decision is still there: a probe trained on agents' own choices reads it (AUROC 0.73 without the instruction), and probes find colluders whose goal was fine-tuned into the weights (AUROC 0.995; pre-registered). We turn the controls into a protocol for testing any collusion monitor, and adapt scan statistics into an online monitor for groups of any size.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 30 pages, 5 figures. Code: https://github.com/mainul3195/collusion-probe-pitfalls ; data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/mainul3195/collusion-probe-pitfalls ; archive: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23636508

Multiagent Systems.title: M3FT: Micro-Macro-Micro Reasoning for Multi-Agent Cryptocurrency Perpetual Futures Trading
Multiagent Systems.summary: Cryptocurrency perpetual futures form a large-scale online financial market in which automated agents manage interacting asset positions under changing conditions. Policies relying solely on micro-level numerical states may overlook cross-asset relationships and become vulnerable to regime shifts, while macro-level linguistic judgments alone cannot ensure precise measurement or optimize positions under trading costs and risk constraints. Connecting market interpretation to coordinated multi-asset decisions remains challenging. We propose M3FT, a micro-macro-micro framework for multi-agent perpetual futures trading. The first micro stage constructs time-aligned numerical states from exchange and account observations through deterministic processing. The macro stage transforms these measured states into explicit market interpretations without adding external market information. Four asset-specific teams, each comprising a Market Interpreter, an Asset Communicator, and a Risk Reviewer, refine these interpretations through experience retrieval, cross-asset communication, and review of joint-position risks. The final micro stage combines encoded linguistic representations with the original numerical states to learn continuous target positions. We implement this framework with a language-conditioned multi-agent policy: asset actors use global and private numerical states together with linguistic context, while centralized critics evaluate joint actions using portfolio-wide information and shared-account rewards. Experiments on real cryptocurrency perpetual futures data, including comparisons across language models and policy-learning algorithms and component ablations, show that the best-performing M3FT configuration achieves a higher mean test return than the evaluated direct LLM, numerical RL, and rule-based baselines.

Multiagent Systems.title: MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks
Multiagent Systems.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.

Multiagent Systems.title: FlowMAS: Learning Multi-Agent Workflow Topology via Information-guided Generative Flow Network
Multiagent Systems.summary: Automated multi-agent systems offer clear advantages over manually designed ones in scalability and adaptability, but existing workflow topology methods still face important limitations. Search-based methods are often computationally expensive, textual-gradient-based methods rely on coarse-grained feedback, and existing generation-based methods are not well suited to discrete workflow topologies with complex dependencies. To address these limitations, we propose FlowMAS, a multi-agent workflow topology method based on Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets). FlowMAS models workflow generation as reward-guided flow over the topology space and introduces three components: a GFlowNet-based topology generation backbone, a curiosity-driven module for structure-aware exploration, and an information-guided optimization module for evaluating intermediate topologies. Concretely, the curiosity-driven module encourages exploration of structurally novel workflows, while the information-guided module measures both the information contribution and the communication efficiency of different operators to favor more informative and effective collaboration patterns. Experiments on six benchmark datasets with three LLM backbones show that FlowMAS consistently outperforms multiple baselines.

Multiagent Systems.title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction
Multiagent Systems.summary: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.

Multiagent Systems.title: LAMaS: A Modular Platform for Learning Low-Latency Multi-Agent Orchestration
Multiagent Systems.summary: In a multi-agent system (MAS), removing an expensive agent call can save tokens without making the answer arrive sooner: latency depends on the longest chain of dependent calls. We present Latency-Aware Multi-agent System (LAMaS), a modular platform for learning low-latency orchestration. A framework can send a query to LAMaS and receive an answer and execution trace, or keep its own graph builder and use the platform's latency-optimized orchestration layer. During training, the layer gives operators on the critical path the greatest latency penalty while targeting a floor on expected accuracy. During inference, a lightweight controller uses partial results to decide whether to skip work that has yet to start. Across four benchmarks, LAMaS reduces end-to-end latency by over 50% relative to the evaluated learning-based MAS baselines while maintaining competitive or better accuracy. GDesigner and AgentDropout retain their graph builders and train the controller on their own traces; both achieve lower latency across the same benchmarks.
Multiagent Systems.comment: Preprint. Previously this version appeared as arXiv:2607.13359 which was submitted as a new work by accident

Multiagent Systems.title: SkillOps: Managing LLM Agent Skill Libraries as Self-Maintaining Software Ecosystems
Multiagent Systems.summary: Large language model agents increasingly rely on skill libraries for multi-step tasks, yet these libraries can accumulate persistent defects as skills are added, reused, patched, and linked to changing dependencies. We call this failure mode skill technical debt: library-level defects that may not break a single skill locally but can harm future retrieval, composition, and execution. Existing skill-based agents mainly focus on task-time retrieval, planning, and repair, while library-time maintenance remains underexplored. We propose SkillOps, a method-agnostic plug-in framework for maintaining skill libraries. SkillOps represents each skill as a typed Skill Contract (P, O, A, V, F), organizes skills with a Hierarchical Skill Ecosystem Graph, and diagnoses library health across utility, compatibility, risk, and validation dimensions. Given a raw skill library, SkillOps produces a maintained library that can be used by existing retrieval or planning agents without changing their internal code. On ALFWorld, SkillOps achieves 79.5 percent task success as a standalone agent, outperforming the strongest baseline by 8.8 percentage points with no additional task-time large language model calls. As a plug-in layer, it improves retrieval-heavy baselines by 0.68 to 2.90 percentage points. The current rule-based maintenance implementation uses nearly zero library-time large language model calls or tokens, showing that skill-library maintenance can be added as a low-overhead architectural layer.

Multiagent Systems.title: Finite-Sample Convergence in Networked Average Reward MARL: Decentralization Pitfalls and Entropy Remedies
Multiagent Systems.summary: We study the problem of average reward Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) where agents interact within a network. Each agent in the network conducts local updates with information within its $k$-hop neighborhood and collaboratively maximizes the overall reward of the entire network. We first provide impossibility results in achieving convergence to the global optimal joint policies in our setting. These impossibility results highlight the challenges of decentralized learning with local information in multi-agent systems, namely the issues of multiagency, where each agent independently optimizes its policy, and partial observability, where agents have limited visibility into the global state. Given these challenges which indicate that decentralized policy optimization can generally be certified only up to stationarity, we provide finite-sample convergence guarantees for a decentralized actor-critic algorithm with linear function approximation that converges to an approximate stationary point with small gradient norm. To overcome such impossibility results, we further show that adding fixed-state entropy regularization reshapes the objective landscape which leads to even stronger global convergence guarantees for our proposed actor-critic algorithm.

Multiagent Systems.title: LSRP*: Scalable and Anytime Planning for Multi-Agent Path Finding with Asynchronous Actions
Multiagent Systems.summary: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) seeks collision-free paths for multiple agents from their respective starting locations to their respective goal locations while minimizing path costs. Although many MAPF algorithms were developed, most of them rely on a common assumption on synchronized actions, where the actions of all agents start at the same time and always take a time unit. This assumption may limit the use of MAPF planners in practice. To get rid of this assumption, recently, an algorithm called Loosely Synchronized Rule-based Planning (LSRP) was proposed, which can find sub-optimal solutions for many agents. However, LSRP often finds poor quality solutions due to its unbounded sub-optimality. This paper develops a new anytime planner called LSRP* that can keep improving solution quality after the initial solution is obtained until the runtime budget depletes. We analyze the properties of LSRP* and test it against several baselines with up to 1000 agents on various maps. LSRP* can handle up to 25% more agents than LSRP and can reduce up to 40% of the solution cost found by LSRP.

Multiagent Systems.title: Scale-Dependent Collective Adaptation in Self-Amending LLM Societies: A Cross-Family Study of Emergent Governance
Multiagent Systems.summary: We study group decision-making in artificial societies where the rules of play are themselves subject to collective amendment. Using the self-amending game Nomic, we compare multiple scales across two LLM families and find that collective adaptation does not improve monotonically with model size. Instead, both families exhibit a narrow mid-scale regime that supports sustained rule adoption, diverse amendments, and balanced consensus. Smaller models tend to remain rule-inert, whereas larger models often converge on restrictive voting patterns, and heterogeneous mixed-size groups collapse into veto-driven gridlock. These cross-scale contrasts persist under temperature perturbations and under a shift from unanimity to majority voting, although latent-state structure varies by family and scale. Hidden-state divergence alone does not explain collective performance: high representational divergence can coincide with poor behavioural outcomes. Linear probes reveal regime-selective coupling between latent vote-predictive signals and collective behaviour, but decodability is necessary rather than sufficient for adaptive play. Overall, the recurring regularity is non-monotonicity, not the particular scale at which the optimum appears. Self-amending games therefore provide a controlled testbed for studying collective adaptation in artificial societies beyond raw model scale.

Multiagent Systems.title: Measuring What Tool-Using LLM Agents Actually Do: Structured Validation, Causal Error Propagation, and Fabricated Tool Use
Multiagent Systems.summary: Tool-using agents built on large language models (LLMs) are usually scored by comparing the final answer with a reference text, using a string heuristic or an LLM judge. This is unreliable when the references describe the task rather than its answer. We replace it with a deterministic validator that checks the tools called, the executed parameters, the resulting state, and whether the values in the answer are supported by the correct tool observations. We re-scored 33,583 traces from 13 agents on simulated calendar, weather, medical and retail tools. The simulator reproduced all 10,396 logged observations, and the gold observations supported the validator in 16 of 18 disagreements with a three-annotator majority (the annotators in none). The instrument changes conclusions: on the same 306 traces, Gemini-2.0-Flash scores 63.4% under the substring heuristic and 5.6% under the validator. In a paired design (same task and model, with and without one schema-valid wrong argument injected into the first tool call), the error rate rises from 52.4% to 74.5% (+22.0 percentage points, 95% CI 18.4-25.5; 1,085 pairs, 7 models), and by 44.7 points (38.4-51.0) where the corrupted call executed without errors. An LLM-judge ensemble estimates +2.5 points on the same pairs. Agents also report tool results without executing any call, in 0-42.5% of traces depending on the model (rule-based lower bounds), largely because the harness accepts an action and a final answer in one completion. A rule-based runtime monitor costs about 7 microseconds per trace but reduces wrong answers mainly by abstaining.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 25 pages, 4 figures. v3: substantially revised. Correctness is now measured by a deterministic gold-grounded validator; the propagation estimate uses a paired causal design. Claims from v1-v2 that were withdrawn or corrected are listed in Section 8. Code and data: https://github.com/bhaskargurram-ai/agenthallu-bench

Multimedia.title: Do Joint Audio-Video Generation Models Understand Physics?
Multimedia.summary: Joint audio-video generation models are rapidly approaching professional production quality, raising a central question: do they understand audio-visual physics, or merely generate plausible sounds and frames that violate real-world consistency? We introduce AV-Phys Bench, a benchmark for evaluating physical commonsense in joint audio-video generation. AV-Phys Bench tests models across three scene categories: Steady State, Event Transition, and Environment Transition. It covers physics-grounded subcategories drawn from real-world scenes, plus Anti-AV-Physics prompts that deliberately request physically inconsistent audio-video behavior. Each generation is evaluated along five dimensions: visual semantic adherence, audio semantic adherence, visual physical commonsense, audio physical commonsense, and cross-modal physical commonsense. Across three proprietary and four open-source models, we find that Seedance 2.0 performs best overall, but all models remain far from robust physical understanding. Performance drops sharply on event-driven and environment-driven transitions, and even strong proprietary systems collapse on Anti-AV-Physics prompts. We further introduce AV-Phys Agent, a ReAct-style evaluator that combines a multimodal language model with deterministic acoustic measurement tools, producing rankings that closely align with human ratings. Our results identify cross-modal physical consistency and transition-driven scene dynamics as key open challenges for joint audio-video generation.
Multimedia.comment: Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ZijunCui/AV-Phys-Bench Code: https://github.com/ZijunCui02/AV-Phys Homepage: https://zijuncui.com/AV-Phys/ Full abstract appears in the PDF

Multimedia.title: Data Diversity, Not Frequency Invariance: A Controlled and Self-Audited Study of Compression-Robust Deepfake Detection
Multimedia.summary: Frequency features and compression-invariant representation learning are widely assumed to be key to deepfake detection that survives video compression. We test this with CAFRL - block-DCT and FFT-phase streams, compression-level-conditioned band attention, and adversarial (gradient-reversal) compression invariance - and report a controlled negative. Under a pre-registered protocol with capacity- and augmentation-matched controls, a plain EfficientNet-B0 on multi-quality data beat CAFRL as specified at every compression level on the FaceForensics++ test split, by 3.66 AUC points at CRF 40 (paired, single seed). A self-audit of our own negative found four defects biased against the frequency hypothesis, and pre-specified re-tests repairing all four showed the deficit to be a recipe artifact, not an architecture failure: the baseline recipe recovered 3.96 points over the matching shipped-recipe variant. The frequency path made no detectable difference: discriminative alone (standalone validation AUC 0.91-0.98 late in training) but of no marginal value under this fusion, at two feature widths of one 4.0 M trunk, every seed-pooled interval for the intra-dataset compression contrasts including zero; on the single held-out manipulation tested, the fair variants sat below the plain backbone. The adversarial branch, as specified, added nothing and degraded its own conditioning estimator; at the fair recipe it is untested. Robustness under single-pass H.264 re-encoding came instead from data diversity: real constant-rate-factor variants beat synthetic JPEG augmentation by 7.3 points (single runs, non-overlapping intervals). The evidence is FaceForensics++-family, GAN-era and single-codec. Match controls on training recipe as well as capacity, and buy compression robustness with codec diversity before architecture.
Multimedia.comment: 38 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to IEEE Access. Code, per-video predictions and a claims-to-artifacts map: https://github.com/Capta1n-n9m0/cafrl-negative (v1.0.0); archival deposit: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22032529

Multimedia.title: MuSP-Bench: Advanced Multimodal Benchmarking of Music Understanding across Score and Performance
Multimedia.summary: Musicians commonly communicate musical intent through scores and performances. To investigate whether models can reason across both modalities, we introduce MuSP-Bench, a human-authored benchmark of 490 questions assessing understanding across Musical Scores and Performances, both individually and in combination. The benchmark spans interpretive and long-horizon reasoning across classical piano and orchestral works, represented through ABC notation, score images, MIDI, and audio. Our evaluation of frontier multimodal large language models reveals substantial difficulties in understanding musical scores and even greater challenges in reasoning about audio.
Multimedia.comment: Accepted to ISMIR 2026 Late-Breaking Demo. Benchmark site: https://musp.vaclis.net/

Multimedia.title: The RenAIssance: Caption-Guided Diffusion Models for Historical-Art Visual Media
Multimedia.summary: Generative AI can expand cultural collections into prompt-responsive visual media, but historical artworks rarely provide the paired descriptions needed to adapt modern image generators. We present The RenAIssance, a scalable pipeline that turns a collection of historical European artworks into a reusable text-to-image media resource. The pipeline generates scene-level captions with BLIP and uses the resulting approximately 15,000 image--text pairs from DEArt to train a compact LoRA adapter for Stable Diffusion v1.5. The adapter shifts generated images toward the historical-art distribution while retaining the base model's ability to render novel concepts. On historical and contemporary prompts of different lengths, it improves FID to the DEArt reference distribution in every setting with only a modest decrease in CLIP text--image similarity. Qualitative results show that the same adapter can render both period-appropriate subjects and contemporary concepts in a coherent historical visual language. By decoupling a reusable style representation from the base generator, the approach offers a practical building block for controllable historical-art media creation, interactive authoring, and rich-media experiences.
Multimedia.comment: Accepted at ACMMM26 RichMediaGAI. This work is co-funded by the European Union's Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under MSCA with grant agreement No 101081674

Multimedia.title: Squeezing Capacity from Multimodal Large Language Models for Subject-driven Generation
Multimedia.summary: Subject-driven image generation aims to synthesize new images that preserve the identity of the given subject while following textual instructions. Existing approaches often encode text and reference images separately. This limits cross-modal reasoning abilities and causes copy-paste artifacts. Recent frameworks that connect multimodal models and diffusion models improve instruction following, but largely overlook identity preservation. To address these limitations, we condition diffusion models on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that jointly encode text and reference images, and augment it with VAE-based identity conditioning. A novel Dual Layer Aggregation (DLA) module is designed to aggregate multi-level MLLM features for optimal conditioning, and a multi-stage denoising strategy is applied to progressively balance the semantic information from MLLM and fine-detail identity from VAE during inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach harmonizes multimodal understanding with identity preservation, mitigates copy-paste issues, and achieves superior performance regarding human preference on subject-driven image generation. Our project website is available at https://zsh2000.github.io/squeeze-mllm-subject-gen/.
Multimedia.comment: NeurIPS 2026, 42 pages, 18 figures, Project Page: https://zsh2000.github.io/squeeze-mllm-subject-gen/

Computational Geometry.title: Latent Reasoning Does Not Lack Signal, It Lacks Invariance: Subspace-Constrained Refinement for Robust Reasoning
Computational Geometry.summary: Latent reasoning models perform multi-step inference in embedding space, reducing the token overhead of chain-of-thought reasoning. Recent training-free refinement methods steer latent trajectories using contrastive signals from stronger and weaker reference checkpoints. We identify three sources of fragility in these methods: hyperparameter sensitivity, reference-pair dependence, and input sensitivity. We propose Trajectory-Invariant Latent Refinement (TILR), a training-free framework that constrains corrections to a stable refinement subspace and adaptively controls their magnitude. First, we extract a spectrally concentrated subspace from strong-weak reference differences across a calibration set and project contrastive updates onto it to filter unstable variation. Second, an adaptive gate scales each update according to its alignment with the learned subspace, suppressing unreliable corrections and recovering the unmodified backbone when alignment is low. Across six reasoning benchmarks, TILR improves robustness to input perturbations and reference selection while maintaining competitive accuracy. On the Coconut backbone, TILR improves answer agreement under semantically equivalent paraphrasing by 11.4% and reduces latent trajectory variance by approximately 30% relative to existing refinement baselines. These results support invariant subspaces as a practical basis for reliable latent refinement without retraining or backpropagation.
Computational Geometry.comment: 18 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Extended version of the previous draft, accepted at the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop. Revised author and affiliation formatting;

Computational Geometry.title: Multiscale Closing Index (MCI) for measuring structural similarity between 2D point sets
Computational Geometry.summary: We introduce Multi-scale Closing Index (MCI), a new dissimilarity measure for evaluating the alignment of two 2D point sets. MCI is bounded between 0 and 1 and is based on multiscale mathematical morphology operations, with smaller values indicating greater structural agreement. The measure was motivated by the need to assess the quality of registration between point sets representing cell populations in biological images. To evaluate its behaviour under controlled conditions, we generated synthetic point clouds from Perlin-noise-based spatial structures, following established approaches for simulating biologically plausible spatial organization. We assessed MCI between those point clouds and different transformed versions, obtained by local perturbation, point removal, translation, rotation and addition of impulsive noise. Across these experiments, the dissimilarity MCI increased gradually and consistently with perturbation severity, while showing a clear discontinuity between clouds originating from the same underlying spatial structure and point clouds generated from different structures. We further compared MCI with commonly used point-set distances, including Hausdorff-based measures and Sliced Wasserstein distance. These experiments show the ability of MCI to capture structural agreement and quantify deviations between point sets, highlighting its potential as a complementary metric for evaluating two-dimensional point-set registration.

Computational Geometry.title: New persistent chain spaces: identifying and computing the relevant persistent Laplacians of a filtration
Computational Geometry.summary: Persistent homology (PH) summarizes the topological features of data that persist across scales, but it is insensitive to many geometric properties. Persistent Laplacians (PLs) address this limitation: for a pair of simplicial complexes in a filtration, the kernel of the persistent Laplacian recovers the persistent Betti number, while its non-zero spectrum carries additional geometric information. However, PLs are defined for individual pairs of filtration values, so analysing a whole filtration requires evaluating many operators that largely contain the same information, and the result is hard to summarize and interpret. In this paper, we show that this redundancy has a precise structure. For each pair of filtration values, we decompose the space of chains underlying the persistent up-Laplacian into the contributions inherited from the neighboring pairs and a remaining part, which we call the new persistent chain space. We show that the new persistent chain spaces of all earlier pairs form a direct sum decomposition of this space, so that every persistent up-Laplacian in the filtration is determined by them. Moreover, the new persistent chain spaces are non-trivial only at pairs given by the persistence pairing in the same and in the next homological dimension, so that the persistence pairing determines exactly where the persistent up-Laplacian can change. Experiments on several types of point clouds show that evaluating persistent Laplacians only at these pairs reduces the computation time, both for our implementation and for existing software.

Computational Geometry.title: Coresets for Capacitated Clustering via Dual Concentration
Computational Geometry.summary:
We study coresets for clustering problems, focusing on the classical $k$-median and $k$-means objectives. A coreset is a small weighted summary of the input data that approximately preserves the clustering cost for every choice of centers. Such summaries are a central tool for scaling clustering algorithms to large datasets.
  In this work, we consider the capacitated setting, where the clustering is subject not only to choosing centers but also to respecting prescribed cluster-size constraints. This model is a natural generalization of standard clustering and has been widely studied, but its coreset complexity is less well understood. For finite metric spaces, we obtain optimal-size coresets; surprisingly, these match the best-known bounds for unconstrained clustering. We also give improved coreset bounds in Euclidean space, notably the first coresets with near-linear dependence in $k$ while being independent of the dimension and input size.
  The main new technical ingredients are concentration bounds for the dual solutions of min-cost flow problems, which allow for both significantly simpler and tighter analyses of the underlying sampling distribution used in the coreset construction.

Computational Geometry.title: Two-colour crossing minimization in complete geometric graphs is NP-hard
Computational Geometry.summary: Given a fixed straight-line drawing of a complete graph, we seek a two-colouring of its edges that minimizes monochromatic crossing pairs. We prove that the threshold decision problem is NP-complete, even for points in general position with integer coordinates. Thus exact minimization is NP-hard, resolving the complexity question posed at the Crossing Number Workshop in 2019. We reduce from MaxCut on permutation graphs by representing source vertices with classes of geometric edges, whose crossings encode source adjacencies. The target complete graph also contains every other edge between its points, and their freely chosen colours can affect the encoded cost. To control these interactions, we construct a large comparison grid with two stable colour phases and use program points to turn this reference into colour preferences on other edges. The optimum differs from a computable baseline plus the amplified minimum number of uncut source edges by an error small enough to distinguish consecutive source values. The reduction is deterministic, with polynomially many points and polynomial coordinate bit length.
Computational Geometry.comment: 34 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Updated author information, presentation and declarations. Proof code and reproducible computations: https://github.com/Myyura/two-colour-crossing-complete-geometric-graphs

Computational Geometry.title: Separating Measures by Hyperplanes
Computational Geometry.summary:
Given red and blue points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, connect every red point to every blue point and weigh each segment by its length under a fixed norm. What fraction of the total weight can always be captured by a single affine hyperplane separating the segments' endpoints? We study this question for finite point configurations in affine general position and, more generally, for pairs of probability measures.
  For dimension one, we show that choosing the best of three thresholds determined by the means of the two distributions captures at least one third of the total red-blue distance. We also give a matching upper bound. Embedding the line construction to higher dimensions shows that the guarantee of $1/3$ cannot be improved for arbitrary measures. Thus, we pivot to the family of measures whose atoms are in affine general position and whose non-atomic part places zero mass on all hyperplanes. Crucially, we establish that the worst-case guarantee is identical for finite configurations in affine general position and several natural classes of probability measures, thereby unifying the discrete and continuous formulations of the problem.
  For this family of measures and for higher dimensions, we extend our guarantee of $1/3$ for all norms. Our proofs combine the ham-sandwich theorem with a novel coupling argument and, in the planar case, an integral representation of norms. We also show that the optimal guarantee improves as the dimension grows, giving a lower bound of $1/2-\operatorname{O}\left(1/\sqrt{d}\right)$ as well as an asymptotically matching upper bound of $1/2$ for every $d$. For the Euclidean distance, we refine the lower bounds to $8/(8+5π)$ and $1/2-\operatorname{O}\left(1/d\right)$ and, for $d=2$, the upper bound to $5/11$. We also derive dimension-dependent guarantees for finite point configurations, including perfect separation of $n$ points of each color when $d\geq2n-1$.

Computational Geometry.title: Containment Problems in Convex Sets
Computational Geometry.summary: Let $P$ be a set of $n$ points in the plane, and let $C$ be a compact, convex subset of the plane that contains the origin in its interior. We study the problem of finding two points $p$ and $q$ of $P$ with the property that any homothet of $C$ that contains $p$ and $q$ must contain at least a constant fraction of the points of $P$. We give proofs for several cases. When $C$ is strictly convex we achieve a fraction of $1/5$, and when $C$ is a general convex region we achieve a fraction of $1/6e$. We show how the ideas of this second bound can be used to prove a lower bound for a version of the problem in $\mathbb{R}^d$ when $C$ is a $d$-ball. We also consider a few special cases. When $C$ is a triangle we get a lower bound of $1/12$, and when we allow that triangle to be rotated by $π$ radians in addition to being scaled and translated we get a lower bound of $1/768$. In proving this last result, we improve the state of the art on the version of this problem in three dimensions, where $C$ is a parallelepiped. We also consider the algorithmic aspects of finding such a pair of points.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Robust Analysis of First-Price Auctions with Large Supply
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
This paper performs a robust analysis of welfare (i.e., the price of anarchy) in multi-unit first-price auctions with independent private values and unit-demand bidders. We employ a smoothness framework (see \citealp{ST-13}) to analyze the price of anarchy when supply is large.
  The main barrier to analysis in this framework is a worst-case bid distribution that establishes a lower bound on the price of anarchy of $1- \frac{1}{e}$. We show that such worst-case distributions cannot arise in equilibrium when agents' values satisfy a mild density lower bound condition. This characterization leads to novel asymptotic lower bounds. In particular, the price of anarchy for $ε$-approximate equilibrium as the number of units goes to infinity is at least $1-Θ\left(ε\log \left(\frac{1}ε\right)\right)$.
  Our analysis relies on a key structural property of equilibrium bid distributions: for a welfare analysis in any multi-unit first-price auction, it is without loss to analyze (approximate) equilibria with no atoms. In addition to this, we establish continuity and monotonicity properties of Bayes-Nash equilibria. We believe these results are of independent interest.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Is Recursive Self-Improvement Safe?
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The phrase recursive self-improvement (RSI) refers to the idea of an AI system designing and creating another, better AI system, which in turn designs and creates an even better one, and so on. While the idea has a long history, it has always been an abstract, futuristic idea -- until recently. Today's frontier AI has attained a set of abilities, including in programming, mathematics, research, tool use, and working coherently over extended periods of time, that make RSI seem plausible. AI companies are starting to pursue it, but many of the involved people are also expressing concerns, asking whether humanity should really set this in motion and under what conditions. I will discuss the situation, argue that we do not even have clear frameworks for thinking about the likely outcomes of RSI, and do a quick game-theoretic analysis of how to choose whether to initiate RSI when another party is making the same choice.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: To appear in IEEE Intelligent Systems

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: FirstSwap: Pre-Consensus Trade Approvals for Decentralized Market Design
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Decentralized exchanges typically give traders no execution guarantee until a block is finalized. In the meantime, external prices move, traders strategically delay submission, and block producers can influence inclusion and ordering. We introduce FirstSwap, a DEX built on a constant-function market maker pricing curve that gives traders an early pre-approval before consensus, guaranteeing inclusion and execution within their submitted price limit, with final ordering determined by limit prices rather than by a block producer.
  We demonstrate the benefits of trade pre-approvals in an economic model combining auction theory with CEX-DEX arbitrage. When the CEX price changes gradually, FirstSwap rewards earlier traders with better prices, discouraging strategic delay and yielding higher social welfare and gains to AMM liquidity providers than a batch auction. When the CEX price jumps abruptly, FirstSwap yields higher welfare and smaller AMM losses than fair ordering.
  The central challenge is delivering fast trade pre-approvals without consensus. We introduce a decentralized, scaled admissibility protocol under which each validator reserves only a fraction of the available liquidity at every price. A trader obtains approval in a single round of messages with a quorum of validators. Somewhat surprisingly, despite Byzantine validators who may approve trades arbitrarily, we show that all quorum-certified trades are jointly admissible and execute within their limits. Our protocol extends naturally to a setting where buy and sell orders can be pre-approved against each other before a block is finalized.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Proportionality in Elections under Feasibility Constraints and Ranked Ballots: The Solid Coalition Refinement Rule
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study elections with ranked ballots and general feasibility constraints, which indicate which sets of candidates are allowed as outcomes. We introduce the first proportionality axiom for this general setting and show that it extends the established notions from specific models that fit our general framework. We extend the Solid Coalition Refinement (SCR) rule to general constraints and prove that it satisfies our axiom exactly for matroid constraints. Although the naive implementation of SCR involves a step that is computationally intractable for weak orders, we show that in practical cases it can be implemented in polynomial time or efficiently in FPT time. We also illustrate limitations of this rule for approval ballots and provide its first empirical evaluation.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Cooperate to Compete: Strategic Data Generation and Incentivization Framework for Coopetitive Cross-Silo Federated Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: In data-sensitive domains such as finance, cross-silo federated learning (CFL) allows organizations to collaboratively train AI models without sharing raw data. However, many practical CFL deployments are coopetitive, where organizations cooperate during model training while competing in downstream markets. In such settings, training contributions can improve the global model yet inadvertently strengthen rivals, eroding one's competitive advantage. This dilemma is amplified by non-IID data, which leads to asymmetric learning gains and undermines sustained participation. While existing work reward organizations based on marginal training contributions, they fail to account for the implicit costs of strengthening competitors. In this paper, we introduce CoCoGen+, a coopetition-compatible data generation and incentivization framework that jointly models data heterogeneity and inter-organizational competition while endogenizing GenAI-based synthetic data generation as a strategic decision. Specifically, CoCoGen+ formulates each training round as a weighted potential game, where organizations strategically decide how much data to generate by balancing learning gains against computational costs and utility losses caused by competition. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the continuous Nash equilibrium under the adopted model and develop a provably convergent scalar bisection algorithm. We further analyze how bilateral payoff redistribution modifies residual competition and data-generation incentives, and empirically evaluate the social welfare and individual utilities of the resulting allocations. Experiments on FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 validate the feasibility of CoCoGen+. The results show how heterogeneity, competition intensity, and incentives shape organizational strategies and social welfare, while CoCoGen+ achieves higher social welfare than competition-aware baselines.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Competition-aware Federated Learning, Strategic data generation approaches, A payoff-redistribution based incentive mechanism, Potential game, Social welfare

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Strategic Competition and Convergence in LLM Leaderboards
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Leaderboards are a popular way to compare large language model (LLM) capabilities and can influence how model developers invest resources. We ask when competition on leaderboards leads developers to produce models with similar capability profiles, which we call monoculture, or similar performance levels. We study this by formulating leaderboard competition as a game in which model developers invest resources across capabilities to maximize their win rate. We show that similar production functions can induce similar capability profiles, while comparative advantage can sustain distinct capability profiles. We then study convergence in performance levels and show that diminishing returns can lead to an increasingly crowded competitive frontier. Using data from LM Arena and OpenRouter, we find that developers improve more in categories where they lag competitors, while still retaining category-specific advantages. At the same time, we find that the frontier of models becomes increasingly crowded, alongside increasingly diversified model usage patterns. Our results suggest that increasing competition does not need to produce interchangeable models, but can instead sustain competitive models with distinct strengths.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Contextual Search and Bilateral Trade with a Trace-Square-Root Potential
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We present a unified potential method for contextual search and bilateral trade with one-bit feedback and obtain order-tight algorithms for both problems. Our framework starts from a Bayesian perspective in which the unknown target (for contextual search) and the unknown pair of valuations (for bilateral trade) are sampled from a known prior distribution. In that model, the decision maker bases its prediction on the posterior distribution, obtained by conditioning on feedback received in previous rounds.
  For Bayesian contextual search, we present an algorithm with a total loss bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt Σ)$, where $Σ$ is the covariance matrix of the target's prior; and for contextual bilateral trade, our algorithm's regret is bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{Σ_S}+\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{Σ_B})$, where $Σ_S$ and $Σ_B$ are the covariance matrices of the seller's and buyer's valuations.
  We then use ideas from this Bayesian setting and adapt a ``dual'' of this trace-square-root potential to the classical worst-case setting, where the target and valuations are chosen adversarially from the unit Euclidean ball. For both contextual search and bilateral trade, we obtain tight $O(\sqrt d)$-regret algorithms. These results match the existing lower bounds up to a constant factor and improve on the previous guarantees of $O(d\log d)$ for contextual search and of $O(d6^d)$ for bilateral trade.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Optimal Regret for Profit Maximization in Bilateral Trade
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Learning to profit from trade requires learning both sides of a market: what a seller is willing to accept and what a buyer is willing to pay. We study repeated bilateral trade, where an intermediary posts a purchase price to a seller and a sale price to a buyer whose valuations are drawn from an unknown joint distribution. Trade occurs only if both parties accept their respective prices, in which case the intermediary earns the difference between the two prices. The intermediary observes only whether trade occurs, without observing either valuation. We show that learning both sides of the market is no harder, in terms of regret, than learning just one. Specifically, we design an algorithm achieving regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3})$ against the best fixed pair of prices, matching, up to logarithmic factors, the classical lower bound for one-dimensional dynamic pricing. Our result shows that the classical one-dimensional regret rate survives the transition to two dimensions, raising the question of whether this absence of a curse of dimensionality extends to arbitrarily high dimensions.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Artificial Shoppers and Attention Competition
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study how AI shopping interfaces affect price competition, platform profit, and consumer welfare. A platform hosts two of three products of different quality. Without AI, consumers compare the hosted pair under salience distortion and overweight whichever attribute, price or quality, stands out. Under assistance, an AI assistant recommends the two products with the highest true utility, leaving consumers to make the same distorted comparison. Under delegation, an AI agent selects the best product, subject to purchase approval. Both modes access all products and know consumers' preferences; firms price strategically. First, assistance can soften competition despite expanded product access. The middle-quality firm may forgo low-valuation consumers because attracting them requires cutting the price paid by higher-valuation consumers as well. Relative to no AI with the same assortment, assistance lowers both hosted prices under the high- and low-quality pair but can raise both under the high- and middle-quality pair. Second, we identify an alignment paradox: some consumers can become worse off than without AI even though their best option remains recommended and becomes cheaper. Salience can induce a switch to a lower-quality product whose quality loss exceeds the saving relative to the original purchase. The assistant ranks products accurately but does not optimize the shortlist for consumers' realized welfare. Third, assistance can raise both platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus with the high- and middle-quality pair; delegation can do so with the high- and low-quality pair. Fourth, among AI designs, the platform weakly prefers delegation with the high- and middle-quality pair wherever all compared pricing equilibria exist. Yet this preferred design can yield lower platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus than the no-AI optimum.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Effective Horizons for Prophet Inequalities with Discounted I.I.D. Rewards
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study prophet inequalities for $n$ i.i.d. base rewards subject to multiplicative discounts across $S$ phases. For equal-length phases and a common discount factor $\widetildeγ$, we characterize the optimal competitive ratio of single-quantile policies as $n\to\infty$ with $S$ and $\widetildeγ$ fixed. The resulting sharp guarantee describes the dependence on the phase parameters: it recovers $1-1/e$ without discounting and approaches $1/2$ in the worst-case regime. We also establish a distribution-free comparison that bounds the discounted prophet by a fractional i.i.d. maximum with effective horizon $B$, the sum of the discount weights across all observations. The comparison yields acceptance probability $1/B$, determined only by the phase profile. This calibration attains the canonical optimum even among single-quantile policies that may choose their acceptance probability using the known base distribution.
