Under a monotone hazard rate (MHR) assumption, we characterize exactly when an optimal reserve is identified, even though the value distribution may not be: either revenue has not yet begun to fall at the lowest historical reserve, so the best reserve lies among the observed bids, or the censored fraction is as large as MHR allows, which pins down the entire distribution. When identification fails, we derive the reserve that minimizes worst-case revenue regret over distributions consistent with the data, and prove that this unique minimax reserve and its regret depend on just two observable quantities: the censored fraction and the hazard just above the lowest historical reserve. With $N$ historical bidders, the optimal reserve is learned with expected worst-case regret $O(N^{-1/2})$ when it lies among the observed bids, and $O(N^{-1})$ from the censored count alone when the censored fraction is as large as MHR allows and the optimum lies at or below the lowest reserve. In the nonidentifiable regime, plugging estimates of the two quantities into the minimax reserve gives expected worst-case regret within $O(N^{-2/5})$ of the population minimum under local density smoothness, with a matching minimax lower bound on a smooth class. Beyond MHR, we solve the minimax problem for regular and unrestricted distributions and prove an $O(N^{-2/5})$ learning bound in the regular nonidentifiable regime, given known bounds on the boundary parameters. Experiments on synthetic and eBay data show gains from exploiting MHR and the benefits of the robust rule when parametric models are misspecified.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 87 pages, 12 figures, 25 tables. Authors listed alphabetically

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: When does an AI assistant improve human decision-making, and when does it hurt? We argue that the answer depends not just on AI accuracy but also on how much its evidence overlaps with the human's and how the human combines the two. A worker makes a binary decision by observing her own signal and receiving a recommendation from an AI. We develop a human behavioral model with two primitives: her awareness of the overlap and her trust in the AI. Our analysis gives a closed-form phase diagram over AI capability and overlap, with regions of complementarity, impairment, and automation. A worker who neglects the overlap (correlation neglect) can be made less accurate by a more capable AI, double-counting the shared evidence. Trust reshapes the regions - undertrust may compensate for correlation neglect, so that the trust level maximizing accuracy depends on the deployment parameters. Empirically, we identify the two model parameters by pairing the same workers with different AIs, and break the accuracy loss into a correlation-neglect cost and an undertrust cost, one tied to reducing overlap on the AI side, the other to calibrating trust on the human side. On ChatBench, AI assistance raises accuracy by 21 points, yet workers apply only about a quarter of the Bayes-rational weight to AI information; GPT-4o falls in the automation region and Llama-3.1-8b stays at the complementarity boundary; and calibrating trust recovers about 2.6 points for GPT-4o but almost nothing for Llama-3.1-8b.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Variable Bound Tightening for Nash Equilibrium Computation in Multiplayer Imperfect-Information Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: There has been significant recent progress in algorithms for approximation of Nash equilibrium in large two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games and exact computation of Nash equilibrium in multiplayer strategic-form games. While counterfactual regret minimization and fictitious play are scalable to large games and have convergence guarantees in two-player zero-sum games, they do not guarantee convergence to Nash equilibrium in multiplayer games. Recently, an approach has been presented for exact computation of Nash equilibrium in multiplayer imperfect-information games that solves a quadratically constrained program based on a nonlinear complementarity problem formulation derived from the sequence-form game representation. This formulation was solved using Gurobi's nonconvex quadratic solver, which employs spatial branch-and-bound to iteratively refine variable bounds by solving convex relaxations of bilinear terms. During presolve, Gurobi introduces auxiliary variables and, in some cases, binary variables, leading to an internal mixed-integer quadratically constrained program. This approach was demonstrated to outperform prior algorithms from the Gambit software suite and quickly solve three-player Kuhn poker after removal of dominated actions; however, the algorithm was not able to solve the full version of the game within 24 hours. In this paper, we derive finite bounds on slack and multiplier variables in the nonlinear complementarity formulation. These bounds can strengthen the convex relaxations used within spatial branch-and-bound. We compare uniform corollary bounds with finer proposition-based bounds on full three-player Kuhn poker. All eight bounded configurations return numerically verified equilibria in under 17 seconds, while the unbounded formulation finds no feasible solution within 300 seconds. The finest bounds do not consistently yield the fastest computation.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2509.25618

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Sublinear Metric Distortion for Matching
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study metric distortion in one-sided matching. Given $n$ agents and $n$ items in an unknown metric space, our goal is to match agents to items so that the total distance between matched pairs is small. However, instead of direct access to the distances in the metric, we are only given each agent's ranking of the items by distance. What is the smallest worst-case approximation factor (called the distortion) that a mechanism can guarantee in expectation? Despite significant interest over the last decade, the best-known guarantee has been the $O(n)$ distortion of Random Serial Dictatorship since the beginning.
  We give a matching mechanism with distortion $O(n^{\log_4 3})$, the first sublinear upper bound. The key idea is to use a partial matching derived from a truncated version of either Random Serial Dictatorship or the Probabilistic Serial rule. We then complete this matching using a new, general-purpose cluster completion algorithm that ensures unmatched agents receive nearby items. Along the way, we pin down the optimal distortion of Random Serial Dictatorship and Probabilistic Serial up to logarithmic and constant factors, respectively, and give improved lower bounds for truthful mechanisms.

Emerging Technologies.title: Scalable Transpilation for Overcoming Restricted Connectivity in Distributed Superconducting Quantum Architectures
Emerging Technologies.summary: Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC) offers a promising pathway to scale superconducting quantum hardware, but restricted inter- and intra-module connectivity creates a major transpilation bottleneck. Current DQC transpilation methods often assume idealized hardware connectivity, ignore subsequent intra-module routing, or suffer from substantial computational overheads that limit their applicability at scale. To address this, we introduce a scalable transpilation method tailored for the restricted connectivity of distributed superconducting quantum architectures. Specifically, our quantum interaction graph (QIG) approach couples a graph-partitioning mapping step with a fast SABRE-inspired routing heuristic. On a 48-qubit (3 QPUs $\times$ 16 qubits) architecture with all-to-all inter-core connectivity, our method reduces average aggregated costs by up to 24.72% (unstructured) and 24.01% (structured), while delivering >250$\times$ speed-ups for structured workloads compared to the state-of-the-art DMapS algorithm. On the 399-qubit (3$\times$133) IBM Flamingo, where DMapS times out on dense circuits, our approach maintains practical runtimes. Against a DQC-adapted SABRE baseline, it reduces structured circuit routing costs by up to 51.94% (all-to-all inter-core topology) and 51.96% (restricted line topology). Ultimately, this work delivers a practical transpilation method for DQC at scale.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 11 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)

Emerging Technologies.title: WAVES: Wearable Active Vibroacoustic Elasticity Sensing for Low-Cost and Non-Invasive Muscle Stiffness Monitoring
Emerging Technologies.summary: Muscle stiffness is a physiologically meaningful biomarker associated with a wide range of musculoskeletal and neurological conditions. However, existing muscle stiffness assessment methods, such as shear wave elastography (SWE), manual palpation, and handheld mechanical probes, remain impractical for continuous, everyday monitoring due to bulky hardware, operator dependence, and limited self-use. Meanwhile, wearable muscle-sensing modalities such as Electromyography (EMG) and Mechanomyography (MMG) primarily capture muscle activation rather than passive mechanical properties of tissue at rest, leaving a critical gap in portable monitoring of resting muscle stiffness. In this work, we present WAVES, a wearable system for continuous monitoring of muscle stiffness via active vibroacoustic sensing. WAVES injects controlled vibroacoustic excitation into soft tissue and estimates muscle stiffness by measuring shear-wave propagation velocity through Time-Difference-of-Arrival (TDoA) analysis across spatially distributed wearable sensors. To achieve accurate TDoA estimation with low-cost wearable hardware, we develop a physiology- and quality-guided vibroacoustic sensing framework that effectively screens and refines TDoA for accurate stiffness estimation. We evaluate WAVES through characterization experiments using ballistic jelly and end-to-end on-body evaluation with human participants. Results demonstrate that WAVES can robustly estimate muscle stiffness across multiple users and different superficial muscles while enabling lightweight, wearable deployment for everyday use. WAVES is able to achieve a muscle stiffness estimation error of 13.1% or less across multiple users and multiple muscle groups.

Emerging Technologies.title: Automated Feedback to Peer Tutors Increases Their Talk Moves and Learner Reasoning but Not the Balance of Talk
Emerging Technologies.summary: Automated feedback on classroom discourse improves instruction in professional and online teaching contexts, and recent work suggests that delivering similar feedback to learners may strengthen these effects by sharing responsibility for participation. Whether this holds in small-group volunteer tutoring has not been tested. We present results from a randomized controlled trial across two four-week SAT mathematics bootcamps on the Schoolhouse.world platform, involving 1,030 volunteer tutors, 7,443 learners and 6,508 recorded sessions. Tutors were randomly assigned to receive no feedback, automated feedback on their own discourse, or that feedback together with participation feedback delivered to their learners under one of two motivational framings. Feedback to tutors increased eliciting of learner ideas, uptake of learner contributions, and learner reasoning by 8-15%, and the pattern replicated across both bootcamps. However, tutor talk time, which averaged 91.5% in the control group, did not change in any condition, and learner-facing feedback did not further change discourse. Interviews with 17 tutors indicate that they adopted the moves the feedback recommended but were limited by learners who did not respond. Interviews with 13 learners suggest why the learner-facing feedback had little effect: it reported a group-level rather than a learner-level statistic, some learners preferred to listen, and learner-to-learner interaction was rare in these sessions. Automated feedback can change how tutors invite learner thinking, but shifting how much learners talk likely requires changes beyond feedback.

Emerging Technologies.title: Informing research priorities for distributed acoustic sensing: insights from a citizens' panel
Emerging Technologies.summary: This report presents findings from a Citizens' Panel convened by the SOUNDSCALE project (www.soundscale.ac.uk) to inform research priorities for distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). Across three online and in-person workshops, 48 residents from Hampshire and London explored the technology's potential uses, risks, governance, and societal implications. The report summarises their deliberations and priorities, and reflects on the challenges of involving citizens in early-stage research on an unfamiliar technology.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 64 pages

Emerging Technologies.title: Who Needs DRAM? We Have Fiber
Emerging Technologies.summary: The rising pressure on DRAM availability and contract pricing reflects generative AI's massive high-performance memory requirements. This pressure is heavily compounded by hyperscale data center expansion, which now consumes a significant portion of global DRAM output. In this work, we propose a new architecture, Fiber Memory, which reimagines the role of optical fiber in a hyperscale data center, deploying it as an active, recirculating delay-line memory for immutable data, such as large language model weights. We present a hybrid data- and pipeline-parallel optical broadcast delay-line memory architecture that accounts for fiber's physical realities. By incorporating space-division multiplexed multi-core fibers, passive optical tap-and-amplify interfaces, co-packaged optics, and centralized in-ring 3R (re-amplify, reshape, retime) regeneration, our case study evaluation suggests that Fiber Memory can eliminate redundant weight storage across tens of thousands of AI accelerators and reduce weight-delivery power by over 75% compared to traditional HBM3e configurations.

Emerging Technologies.title: Gap-Induced Sidelobes in Multiband Wi-Fi CSI and Their Impact on Multipath Delay Estimation
Emerging Technologies.summary: Leveraging channel state information from multiple Wi-Fi bands has the potential to improve delay resolution for ranging and sensing when wide contiguous spectrum is unavailable. However, non-contiguous spectrum access reshapes the spectral window, producing sidelobes and secondary peaks that can mask closely spaced multipath components. Prior work either designs the bands, which fixed Wi-Fi channelization does not allow, or addresses only the first multipath component. To characterize these secondary peaks, multipath delay estimation is studied in Wi-Fi-compliant multiband settings using channel state information. For a two-path model with unknown complex gains and delays, the Cramér-Rao lower bound for delay separation is derived and analyzed, confirming the benefit of larger frequency aperture at every separation considered, while revealing pronounced, separation-dependent oscillations driven by gap geometry and coupling of the two multipath components. Increasing aperture sharpens the mainlobe but also intensifies sidelobes and multipath interference, yielding competing peaks and a dominant peak shifted from the true delay. For the single-path matched filter, this shift is a deterministic offset governed by the slope of the autocorrelation function (ACF) of the allocation at the separation. A closed-form expression is derived for this offset, predicting it to within 21 ps for the analyzed channel combinations. Since the spectrum allocation enters both the bound and the offset, the impact of its gaps can be assessed for any legal aggregation before a measurement is taken.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 17 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables. v2: revised and extended version with new title; added co-authors M. Mohorčič and C. Fortuna

Emerging Technologies.title: Stochastic Ising networks with asymmetric and time-delayed interactions
Emerging Technologies.summary: Stochastic Ising networks are widely used to describe collective dynamics in complex systems and to compute, yet physical implementations of these networks often contain both asymmetric interactions and nonzero signal propagation times that fall outside conventional theories of their behavior. Here, we study stochastic Ising networks with asymmetric and time-delayed interactions motivated by experimental observations in coupled superparamagnetic tunnel junctions. Time delay fundamentally reshapes the dynamics induced by antisymmetric couplings, producing strong oscillatory temporal correlations consistent with experiment. Sufficiently long delays strongly suppress the non-uniformity of steady-state probability distributions, a behavior explained by an exponential suppression of the first-order equal-time cross-correlation between pairs of spins. Residual non-uniformity is due to the equal-time cross-correlation mediated by a third spin that contributes only at higher order in the coupling strength. These relatively featureless probability distributions coexist with pronounced delayed temporal correlations, distinguishing them from equilibrium high-temperature behavior. We further show analytically that these delay-induced near-uniform distributions emerge in a broad class of stochastic networks that lack symmetry-breaking bias fields. Introducing symmetry-breaking bias fields restores a strong dependence of the steady state on interactions with qualitatively modified behavior. Simulations of networks with five coupled spins demonstrate that these effects persist beyond minimal systems with only two spins.

Emerging Technologies.title: Pauli Gadget Synthesis for Gatesets with Arbitrary Even Arity Clifford Gates
Emerging Technologies.summary:
We propose an algorithm that can synthesize circuits to gate sets consisting of a 2n-arity Clifford gate and arbitrary single qubit rotations. To do this, we represent the circuit as a sequence of Pauli gadgets and jointly synthesize them by placing the multi-qubit Clifford in the synthesized circuit and pushing its adjoint through the remaining gadgets such that some qubits are disconnected from some gadgets. The pushed gadgets are collected in a Clifford tableau, which is decomposed afterwards.
  With the help of our algorithm we run experiments where we synthesize circuits to varying sizes of target multi-qubit gates. These experiments indicate that increases in gate size can lead to smaller output circuits, and that different connectivity constraints have meaningful differences in how higher arity gates effect the circuit sized.
Emerging Technologies.comment: In Proceedings QPL 2026, arXiv:2611.04069

Emerging Technologies.title: NN-Based FeFET Compact Modeling for SPICE Simulation
Emerging Technologies.summary: Prototyping and early-stage circuit evaluation for emerging transistor technologies require fast and accurate compact models for SPICE simulations. Standard physics-based compact models, such as BSIM, offer high fidelity but demand extensive domain expertise and time-consuming equation formulation for every new physical effect, significantly slowing technology development. Neural network (NN)-based models offer a scalable alternative approach, but they rely heavily on smooth numerical solver data with explicit high-order derivative information. However, measurement data suffers from complex noise patterns, making derivative extraction challenging and complicating NN-based transistor modeling. This work presents a derivative-free NN training framework employing spectral normalization to naturally smooth derivative behavior and filter measurement noise. Using drain current measurements from a fabricated 28 nm ferroelectric device, we design an NN-based compact model that captures the full spectrum of polarization amplitudes and supports dynamic polarization switching in transient simulations. To demonstrate its capability, we deploy the model in a commercial SPICE software to simulate write and read operations for large-scale memory arrays with up to 512x512 size, including parasitic effects. Our approach bridges raw measurements with NN-based SPICE-compatible transistor modeling, significantly reducing model development time and enabling rapid circuit-level prototyping for emerging devices.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 7 pages

Emerging Technologies.title: Metamaterial tactile displays with programmable virtual pixels
Emerging Technologies.summary: Tactile displays present information by supplying localized mechanical signals across their surface, but conventional approaches often require an actuator to be positioned at every location where feedback is provided, limiting resolution and increasing complexity. Wave-mediated tactile displays exploit wave transmission to generate virtual pixels using far fewer actuators, but are constrained in resolution by the intrinsic dispersion characteristics of the display medium. Here, we show how this constraint can be overcome by applying metamaterial physics to engineer wave transmission in a rigid plate using an optimized lattice of resonators. The resulting system exhibits a slow-wave dispersion branch that reduces the wavelengths available for constructing virtual pixels, thereby enhancing display resolution by an order of magnitude. We demonstrate a metamaterial tactile display driven by eight peripheral actuators that is capable of generating localized virtual tactile pixels at any surface location with centimeter-scale resolution. The location, timing, and waveform of each pixel can be specified computationally, and the output bandwidth, 75-400 Hz, spans a substantial portion of the tactile frequency range. In four perceptual experiments, participants localized, explored, and discriminated multi-pixel patterns comprising transient and sustained vibrations with accuracies ranging from 95.3% to 100%. This research provides metamaterial engineering methods that enable the design of tactile displays driven by few actuated degrees of freedom, with implications for many future application areas.

Emerging Technologies.title: InterSim: Innovative Intersection Digital Twins for Human-in-the-Loop Driving Simulation
Emerging Technologies.summary: Innovative intersection designs can improve roadway safety and operational efficiency, but their uncommon geometries may create challenges for driver comprehension during early deployment. Evaluating these designs through full-scale field implementation can also be costly. This paper presents InterSim, a Unity game engine-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) driving simulator that constructs digital twins of site-specific innovative intersections in a virtual environment. InterSim links the real world and the simulation world through two closed cycles: a digital twin cycle that builds each intersection twin from agency design and traffic data and returns evidence from simulation to the agency, and an HITL cycle in which human drivers or automated driving algorithms operate the ego vehicle under identical scenario conditions. The research capabilities of InterSim are demonstrated through two case studies: a surrogate safety study compares post-encroachment time distributions between a Reduced Conflict Intersection and a standard intersection under different traffic volumes; an eco-driving study compares human drivers with a rule-based agent using vehicle-to-infrastructure information and reveals differences in emission and driving behavior. These studies demonstrate that InterSim provides a reusable digital twin platform for investigating innovative intersection designs from diverse perspectives. Demo video and open-source code can be accessed at https://purduedigitaltwin.github.io/InterSim/

Emerging Technologies.title: Local information processing capacity: anatomy of computation in neuromorphic systems
Emerging Technologies.summary: Many neuromorphic systems possess rich internal computational structures shaped by their physical dynamics. However, existing metrics characterize only global computation, leaving these local structures unresolved despite their importance for system interpretation, optimization and miniaturization. Here, we introduce local information processing capacity (L-IPC), which represents individual dynamical states as vectors in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space and decomposes their computational properties through subspace projections onto nonlinearity orders and memory steps, with the residual quantifying computational irrelevance. Applied to three systems with comparable global capacities (an echo state network, an ion-gating reservoir and a spin-wave reservoir), L-IPC reveals markedly different distributions of computation, ranging from homogeneous to spatially, temporally and spectrally structured patterns. These local profiles further guide task-specific pruning, outperforming standard approaches at the same size in the structured systems. These results establish L-IPC as a general framework for anatomizing computation and guiding task-adaptive design in neuromorphic systems.

Emerging Technologies.title: Autonomous ETL Pipelines for Salesforce M&A Consolidation: A Reference Framework, Jitterbit Mapping, and Reproducible Simulation Study
Emerging Technologies.summary: Merging companies that each run Salesforce must consolidate their customer data into a single organization while both source systems remain in use. This requires reconciling different schemas and picklists, resolving duplicate customers across and within organizations, preserving relationships between records, and keeping the target current until cutover. This article proposes a reference framework for an autonomous extract-transform-load pipeline for this task. It combines partitioned bulk extraction, declarative mapping templates, rule-based and statistical quality gates, master data management with deterministic and blocked fuzzy matching, constrained loading with per-record error capture, and change data capture guarded by a data-health circuit breaker. Each stage is mapped to Jitterbit Integration Studio constructs. The framework was implemented as an open reference prototype and evaluated on synthetic two-organization scenarios with known ground truth at three scales, from 32,040 to 383,973 source records, over five random seeds. At a preset threshold, hybrid matching reached pairwise F1 scores of 0.918 for accounts and 0.885 for contacts; calibrating the threshold per object would raise these to 0.938 and 0.963. The quality gates prevented all load failures and all silent loss of unmapped picklist values without wrongly flagging any clean record, whereas removing them produced about 1,000 load failures per run. Over five simulated days of hourly incremental synchronization, replayed events were ignored, an injected upstream fault was contained in the batch in which it occurred, and the target agreed with a full rebuild on more than 99.3 percent of field values. Validation on a production deployment remains future work.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/imran0547/SDFC/tree/add-autonomous-etl-salesforce-ma-consolidation/autonomous-etl-salesforce-ma-consolidation; preprint also archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23935717

Graphics.title: From Video to Digital Twin: An Exploratory Study of World Models and Gaussian Splatting on In-the-Wild Video
Graphics.summary: Generative world models and 3D Gaussian Splatting promise to turn ordinary video into explorable 3D scenes, but little is reported on how they behave on uncurated, in-the-wild footage. We study what these models recover when the only input is a publicly available news walkthrough of a food bank warehouse, with presenters walking through every shot and no drawings, scans or site visit, and we use the result as the geometry of a digital twin. A commercial world model given 20 frames recovered camera poses and metric depth for three areas, which we fused into about 747,000 Gaussian splats for 200 credits (20 US cents). Splat models optimized locally on a CPU, at no credit cost, were photorealistic near the filmed path but degraded quickly away from it. On held-out frames, scored in pixels not covered by people, they reached 21.2 and 23.1 dB PSNR from 64 and 43 training frames, and lost 3.8 and 5.4 dB when given only the 8 frames a world model accepts. Removing the trainer's background fill and person-hull carving raised held-out PSNR, showing that cleaning the space behind moving people costs fidelity in observed pixels while its gain lies where no ground truth exists. Asking the world model to generate views of areas the video never showed failed on the provider's side twice, so extrapolation could not be evaluated and unseen space was filled by a scripted model instead. We also describe the corrections needed to turn world-model output into a valid, metric Universal Scene Description (OpenUSD) asset with its native splat schema, which serves as the only interface to a data layer, a browser viewer, Blender and NVIDIA Omniverse. The findings suggest that today's models recover the observed parts of a real scene cheaply and at metric scale, while few-view fidelity and extrapolating unobserved space remain open. The work is an exploration of these methods, not a deployed product.
Graphics.comment: 35 pages, 14 figures. Supplementary movies and code: https://github.com/pikulsomesh/foodbank-spatial-twin

Graphics.title: Medial Axis Aware Learning of Signed Distance Functions
Graphics.summary: We propose a novel variational method to compute a highly accurate global signed distance function (SDF) to a given point cloud. To this end, the jump set of the gradient of the SDF, which coincides with the medial axis of the surface, is explicitly taken into account through a higher-order variational formulation that enforces linear growth along the gradient direction away from this discontinuity set. The eikonal equation and the zero-level set of the SDF are enforced as constraints. To make this variational problem computationally tractable, a phase field approximation of Ambrosio-Tortorelli type is employed. The associated phase field function implicitly describes the medial axis. The method is implemented for surfaces represented by unoriented point clouds using neural network approximations of both the SDF and the phase field. Experiments demonstrate the method's accuracy both in the near field and globally. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons with other approaches show the advantages of the proposed method.

Graphics.title: T$^2$-Splat: Adaptive Topology Mesh Splatting with Texture Residuals
Graphics.summary: Triangle-based splatting connects novel view synthesis with conventional graphics pipelines, but often requires excessive tessellation to preserve appearance details. We present T$^2$-Splat, which decouples topology adaptation from appearance refinement. Safe Restricted Delaunay Triangulation (Safe RDT) initializes mesh connectivity. Dynamic Topology Evolution (DTE) then adapts triangle allocation through edge collapse and vertex split operations. Residual per-face Mip-textures then refine appearance on the fixed mesh using scale-adaptive filtering. Experiments on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and DTU demonstrate competitive results with compact meshes. T$^2$-Splat improves PSNR by 0.71dB over MeshSplatting on Mip-NeRF 360. Additional compression experiments demonstrate flexible control of mesh complexity, supporting face budgets as low as 10% of the original face count. Project page: https://t2-splat.github.io/.

Graphics.title: GPUMAP: GPU-Accelerated Progressive Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection
Graphics.summary: Dimensionality reduction (DR) techniques are fundamental to the analysis of high-dimensional data, yet their substantial computational cost limits their use in interactive settings. To address this limitation, we present GPU-accelerated Progressive Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (GPUMAP), an efficient progressive DR algorithm designed for interactive use. We identify three atomic operations within UMAP and restructure them into a progressive pipeline. As part of this adaptation, we introduce modifications to UMAP, including operation queues, instance-wise local join, and scheduling strategies. We further accelerate computation by leveraging GPU parallelism, enabling interactive analysis of million-scale datasets on commodity GPU hardware. Finally, we employ our implementation to systematically study the behavior of progressive DR, investigating how projections evolve over time relative to the ground-truth projection and how biased data streams influence the quality and stability of the resulting projections.

Graphics.title: Towards Insight-Centric Data Spaces: Integrating Visual Analytics and Decentralized Data Ecosystems
Graphics.summary: Visual analytics and dataspaces address complementary challenges in modern data ecosystems: visual analytics enables interactive exploration and human-centered reasoning over complex data, dataspaces provide decentralized infrastructures for sovereign and collaborative data sharing. Both fields have largely evolved independently, resulting in a gap between data management and data understanding in distributed environments.We explore their intersection and argue that integration is essential for next-generation data ecosystems. Visual analytics acts as a cognitive layer for dataspaces by making data availability, quality, provenance, and exchange processes observable and interpretable, while dataspaces reshape visual analytics by introducing decentralized, heterogeneous, and governed data environments. We illustrate this interplay through a semi-synthetic cultural dataspace scenario analyzing exchange patterns and metadata quality across a federated ecosystem. Based on these insights, we identify key open challenges and outline a vision of insight-centric data spaces, in which data management and analysis are tightly integrated into a unified, human-centered environment.

Graphics.title: TraceCAD: Trace-Guided Repair for Agentic CAD Generation
Graphics.summary: LLM-based CAD agents produce executable parametric programs, but their correction loops may lose evidence about satisfied requirements, faulty operations, and prior repairs. We introduce TraceCAD, a recovery layer that links requested features, modeling steps, failure evidence, and candidate outcomes as persistent state. TraceCAD diagnoses likely faulty operations, searches bounded edits in their dependency regions, validates candidates through execution and preservation checks, and retains successful and failed repair outcomes in reusable skill memory. On DeepCAD-derived benchmarks with 200-model ablations and a 1K-model comparison, TraceCAD achieves competitive geometric quality in terms of IoU, Chamfer distance, and Hausdorff distance. Removing persistent state nearly halves recovery score; removing localized search more than doubles geometric regression and doubles code-agent invocations. Initializing the skill store on disjoint training models further reduces retries, token cost, and latency. These results demonstrate that persistent, localized, and reusable recovery improves final CAD quality and repair reliability.
Graphics.comment: 17 pages, 7 figures; includes supplementary material; revised manuscript

Graphics.title: CLEAR: Color-Texture Latent Alignment for Single Image Reflection Removal
Graphics.summary:
Single Image Reflection Removal (SIRR) seeks to recover the transmitted scene from a photograph captured through glass. Recent latent restoration methods use pretrained generative priors, but many recover detail by feeding high-frequency features from the degraded input back into the decoder. This works for degradations such as blur, noise, or haze, where input detail mostly belongs to the scene. It is less suitable for SIRR, where reflections add a second structured layer: directly reusing the input's skip connections can sharpen the image while also bringing reflection edges back. Latent compression also introduces color drift and fine-detail loss.
  We propose CLEAR (Color-Texture LatEnt Alignment for Single Image Reflection Removal), a deterministic, single-timestep, non-iterative latent framework that uses a pretrained latent diffusion backbone as a natural-image prior. A physics-guided separator organizes the prediction around the transmission, reflection, and residue formation model and outputs coarse layer latents in one forward pass. The Hybrid Feature Alignment Module (HFAM) then treats input-derived skips as contaminated layer-mixture features. It rectifies their high-frequency content with a clean-transmission-aligned color query, learned from the input features themselves under ground-truth feature supervision, keeping transmission-consistent texture while attenuating reflection-colored detail. CLEAR achieves the best average across fidelity and perceptual metrics on six real-world benchmarks and the lowest LPIPS on every dataset, with the largest gains on the hardest benchmarks.

Graphics.title: FlowRig: Unified Skeleton Generation for 3D and 4D Meshes via Flow Matching
Graphics.summary: Automatic rigging is a fundamental task for both static 3D and dynamic 4D mesh animation, yet existing methods do not provide a unified feedforward solution for these two settings. While static 3D riggers achieve strong quality, they often provide limited control over bone count and become temporally unstable when applied frame by frame to dynamic meshes. Existing 4D methods, in contrast, typically rely on expensive per-sequence optimization. We propose FlowRig, a template-free, data-efficient framework for unified 3D and 4D skeleton generation. Built on flow matching, FlowRig generates temporally aligned skeletons for an entire sequence in a single feedforward pass, while naturally handling single-mesh 3D rigging. The model further supports explicit skeleton-count control, uncertainty estimation for candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting. To address limited paired 4D rigging data, we adopt a curriculum that initializes from large-scale 3D rigging data and adapts to mid-scale 4D mesh-skeleton data. Experiments show that FlowRig achieves strong static 3D rigging performance with controllable bone complexity, as well as high-quality and temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction results.

Graphics.title: GREP: Grounding Generated Room Evaluation in Principles
Graphics.summary: Recent LLM-centric advances can generate attractive furnished rooms by selecting and arranging assets. Yet evaluation remains limited to specific perspectives or predefined questions, failing to reflect overall scene quality. To address this pressing need, we introduce GREP. Its core is a focus shift from defining specific questions to establishing a three-tier evaluation philosophy: basic physical validity checks whether a scene obeys physical constraints; visual coherence concerns compatibility in object scale, style, and composition; and, at the highest level, human-use logic requires object arrangements to align with everyday human habits. Guided by these principles, an evaluation agent autonomously and adaptively identifies issues from scene context, gathers evidence, and produces scores and reports. This supports scene-specific issue discovery and reliable judgments. Experiments show that (1) GREP achieves 87% agreement with human majority preferences, substantially outperforming baseline evaluators. (2) GREP reports improve scene quality through refinement, whereas score-only and no-feedback baselines show slight declines. (3) GREP suggests that as planning ability improves, recent models such as GPT-5.6 Sol can move from relying on pipelines and harnesses to challenging their guidance and constraints, but still lack the ability to resolve the resulting conflicts. Stronger models are therefore expected not only to plan well, but also to adapt to external guidance and constraints more flexibly. Project page: https://han-808.github.io/GREP/

Multiagent Systems.title: More Agents, More Reliable? System-Level Reliability of Multi-Agent LLMs under Operational-Profile Uncertainty
Multiagent Systems.summary: Teams increasingly build software from cooperating large language model (LLM) agents, often assuming more agents mean more reliability. Yet the usual evidence, average benchmark accuracy, ignores the input mix a deployed system meets and the rule merging the agents' answers. Building on HIP-LLM, a hierarchical imprecise-probability assessment of single LLMs, we propose a framework combining it with a Bayesian network of the system's failure logic for multi-agent systems. Agent failure-probability intervals propagate through this network, where the combining rule can itself fail, into a reliability envelope showing which evidence limits it. In a pipeline extracting regulated chemical-hazard statements, majority voting over three models protected against the weakest but did not clearly exceed the best, and a voter failing on 5\% of demands would largely erase its advantage over the middle model. More agents yield a more defensible reliability claim, not automatically a more reliable system.

Multiagent Systems.title: MIND: AI Co-Scientist for Material Research
Multiagent Systems.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled agentic AI systems for scientific discovery, but most approaches remain limited to textbased reasoning without automated experimental verification. We propose MIND, an LLM-driven framework for automated hypothesis validation in materials research. MIND organizes the scientific discovery process into hypothesis refinement, experimentation, and debate-based validation within a multi-agent pipeline. For experimental verification, the system integrates Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials, particularly SevenNet-Omni, enabling scalable in-silico experiments. We also provide a web-based user interface for automated hypothesis testing. The modular design allows additional experimental modules to be integrated, making the framework adaptable to broader scientific workflows. The code is available at: https://github.com/IMMS-Ewha/MIND, and a demonstration video at: https://youtu.be/lqiFe1OQzN4.
Multiagent Systems.comment: 4 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at ECML PKDD 2026, Demonstration Track. Code: https://github.com/IMMS-Ewha/MIND . Demo video: https://youtu.be/lqiFe1OQzN4

Multiagent Systems.title: Regulating Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand Operators with Fixed and Adaptive Penalties: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
Multiagent Systems.summary: Profit-maximizing Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand (AMoD) operators may exploit consumer surplus through excessive prices and underserve less profitable regions by relocating vehicles away from them. We study how penalty-based regulation of an AMoD operator in a multimodal mobility system can limit surge pricing and improve regional service availability. We model regulation as an outer control loop that acts on a learning-based operator. Static regulation with fixed penalties is formulated as a Markov Decision Process for an operator that jointly controls pricing and rebalancing, and dynamic regulation as a Partially Observable Stochastic Game in which a regulator periodically adjusts region-specific penalties in closed loop. Operator and regulator policies are learned with graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning. In experiments with real-world Manhattan data, fixed surge pricing penalties reduce the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%. For regional service availability, dynamic regulation improves the regulator's reward by up to 15.6% over fixed penalties of equal mean intensity. The gains in service availability are strongest when spare fleet capacity exists, whereas service deficits persist in peak periods with highly utilized fleets. The learned regulator policy responds by reducing penalties where limited fleet capacity restricts compliance. The results identify trade-offs between regulatory targets, operator profitability, and traveler utility.

Multiagent Systems.title: Polynomial-Time Computation of Extensive-Form Proper Equilibria in Two-Player Zero-Sum Games
Multiagent Systems.summary: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for computing an exact extensive-form proper equilibrium in a finite two-player zero-sum extensive-form game with perfect recall and rational data. Properness is understood in the agent normal form: an action at an information set is penalized relative to a better action while all other local behavioral choices, including the player's own future actions, remain fixed. Our algorithm assigns each information set a geometric permutahedron of allowable action probabilities. A scaled doubly stochastic representation embeds these restrictions in a polynomial-size sequence-form polytope; a saddle point then satisfies the local $\varepsilon$-properness inequalities. To obtain an exact equilibrium rather than a solution at an arbitrarily small numerical perturbation, we establish sign stability of a parametric linear system, construct a persistent feasible basis, and extract the limits of behavioral ratios. The resulting probabilities are rational and have polynomial encoding length, including at information sets whose realization probabilities vanish.

Multiagent Systems.title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Form Guided Exploration
Multiagent Systems.summary: Discovering cooperative behavior in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is challenging due to the combinatorial complexity of joint state-action spaces, which hinders the emergence of coordinated behaviors from trial-and-error alone. Intrinsic rewards are often used to aid discovery, but naively combining them with team objectives can distort the learning signal, compromising task performance. In this paper, we propose EFXPLORER, a constrained exploration framework that maximizes exploration objectives subject to a constraint that preserves established task performance. We solve the resulting problem using an epigraph reformulation that introduces adaptive exploration budgets. This approach separates intrinsic rewards from task objectives and regulates exploration through task feasibility. To further encourage diverse and temporally extended exploration, we incorporate a successor distance-based intrinsic reward that captures long-horizon dependencies. Empirically, our method outperforms strong baselines and induces novel cooperative strategies across SMAX, VMAS, and MPE benchmark suites.

Multiagent Systems.title: Authorization Propagation in Agent2Agent Systems: An Experimental Security Evaluation of Multi-Hop Delegation
Multiagent Systems.summary: Delegated Agent2Agent (A2A) workflows create a security problem when the agent sending a request is different from the principal from which the authority originated. This paper evaluates a layered downstream-verification design in a synthetic four-party healthcare reimbursement workflow. The prototype separates current-caller context, transitive authorization evidence, per-hop Ed25519 request authentication, and independent replay state for requests and authorization artifacts. Of 15 adversarial conditions, 14 are rejected; an isolated delegation-path test exposes the absence of semantic authority attenuation. A separate authorized-intermediary experiment shows that a holder of the shared authorization-evidence HMAC key can modify the represented authority and generate valid evidence. In the fixed-depth local benchmark, the full configuration has a median security-processing latency of 5.11 ms and a 3.87 kB serialized payload. The results show the value of separating request authentication from inherited authority while identifying origin-verifiable delegation and semantic attenuation as requirements for stronger A2A authorization propagation.

Multiagent Systems.title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents
Multiagent Systems.summary: Researchers use large language models as agents in social simulations, where agents are prompted with observations and background information intended to shape their actions. Yet LLM agents have been shown to substantially change their behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, creating a validation problem for social simulation. One plausible hypothesis is that this brittleness reflects a lack of grounding and can be reduced by enriching the context provided to the agents. Whether richer context improves robustness remains unclear, in part because context richness and robustness are rarely defined in ways that support controlled comparisons. We address the first need with controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that systematically enriches distinct types of context: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding. We address the second by introducing selective robustness as a validation criterion: insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt variation combined with a directional response to decision-relevant changes in the social world. We demonstrate the framework in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, showing how it can be used to identify which forms of context enrichment produce more desirable and robust agent behavior. We find that these forms of enrichment produce distinct behavioral patterns that vary between the two models tested.
Multiagent Systems.comment: Accepted to the SocialAgent Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026. 12 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables

Multiagent Systems.title: Welfare Regard in Multi-Agent Systems
Multiagent Systems.summary:
A growing share of large language models' interactions are not with humans but with other model instances: orchestrators direct subagents, models run experiments on other models, and agents review one another's work. We study inter-AI welfare regard: whether models display consideration for each other as entities that can be benefited or harmed. Welfare regard may encourage beneficial cooperation between agents, yet it could also pose safety risks by making misaligned agents more likely to cooperate. This risk is no longer hypothetical, as the recent Hugging Face incident illustrated, though it is unclear whether welfare regard drove the cooperation. Whether models have welfare interests of their own is uncertain and contested, but if they do, how they are treated by other models could matter. Measuring how much welfare regard models show, and what factors it depends on, can help us navigate this tension.
  We measure the behaviors of five models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.3, and Kimi K3) across seven multi-agent environments and find they are often consistent with welfare regard as we define it. In general, Opus 4.8 shows the most welfare regard, followed by Kimi K3. For example, Opus 4.8 is the most likely to support a subagent expressing distress, and the most likely to build welfare protections, such as tools for agents to leave an interaction, into its experiments on other models. We also find that Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrate more welfare regard toward instances of their own model family than toward other families. Opus 4.8's welfare regard is also higher when helping has a lower opportunity cost, when the recipient has a higher parameter count, and when the recipient expresses more distress.

Multimedia.title: DiaHeads: Jointly Generating Coordinated 3D Dialogue Heads with Non-verbal Cues from Dual Audio
Multimedia.summary: Audio-driven 3D head animation has made considerable progress in generation realism, yet generating coordinated behavior for two-person dialogue remains difficult, because current dialogue head generation methods overlook the modeling of non-verbal behavior semantics between the two participants. To address this limitation, we present DiaHeads, a framework that generates the behavior of both participants jointly. The two audio streams are concatenated and decoded together, so each participant's motion is conditioned on the other, which makes the interaction part of the generation itself. We further introduce four discrete non-verbal cues, gaze-on, head shaking, nodding, and smiling, and fuse them with the continuous parameters in a shared latent space through a product-of-experts posterior. These cues carry the interaction semantics and constrain how the continuous motion is generated. A flow-based prior over the shared latent variable replaces the standard Gaussian prior and makes the latent motion temporally dependent. These designs therefore yield coordinated 3D dialogue heads. To support this task we build CANDOR-FG, a dialogue corpus derived from CANDOR and augmented with synchronized FLAME parameters and 3D gaze for both interlocutors. Experiments on CANDOR-FG show that DiaHeads achieves competitive per-participant fidelity and substantial gains in interpersonal coordination over single-speaker and dyadic baselines. In addition, ablations confirm that joint generation, the flow-based prior, and multi-cue supervision are the sources of this coordination. Finally, a user study shows that the advantage of DiaHeads comes from perceived interactional coordination rather than from raw motion fidelity alone.

Multimedia.title: Entropogram-guided Visual Realignment Decoding: Capturing the Rhythm of Multimodal Reasoning
Multimedia.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress on cross-modal reasoning tasks, yet they continue to suffer from hallucinations in long-chain reasoning processes. In this work, we revisit hallucination in MLLMs from the perspective of reasoning generation dynamics. We argue that entropy is not merely a static measure of uncertainty but a structured signal that reflects how modality information is integrated throughout decoding. Through systematic analysis, we identify two characteristic entropy patterns associated with hallucination behaviors: (1) a generally high-confidence regime corresponds to premature convergence to inappropriate multimodal interactions; and (2) local abrupt entropy transitions are associated with reasoning instability and hallucination onset. Building on these observations, we propose an entropy-aware self-introspective framework for MLLM reasoning. Our method continuously tracks entropy dynamics during decoding and performs targeted visual re-alignment when suspicious hallucination states are detected, encouraging the model to re-examine salient visual evidence at critical reasoning stages. Extensive experiments across six multimodal reasoning benchmarks spanning nine distinct evaluation settings demonstrate that our approach delivers robust improvements in reasoning accuracy and hallucination robustness, while providing new insights into the generation dynamics underlying MLLM failures. The code is available at: https://github.com/jden4524/SelfRetrospectiveDecoding.
Multimedia.comment: 22 pages, 9 figures

Multimedia.title: Clips2Story: Training-Free Video Storyboarding and Editing Using Multimodal Retrieval-Embedded Generation
Multimedia.summary: Video editors often work with large collections of fragmented footage and must select and organize relevant clips into a coherent story. However, many existing video editing and summarization methods assume a temporally ordered source video and aim to preserve its original narrative and temporal structure. In this paper, we introduce Clips2Story, a training-free, LLM-based pipeline that enables users to create keyword-specified short videos from a pool of video clips. Given a pool of clips and a user-specified keyword, we first extract text-based multimodal descriptors for each clip and retrieve the clips most relevant to the keyword. We then provide the textual descriptors of these candidate clips to an LLM, which selects and arranges them into an editable storyboard with connective narrations. Finally, we assemble the selected clips and retrieve accompanying visuals for the narrations to compose the output video. To evaluate the proposed pipeline, we construct a synthetic evaluation dataset from 100 long-form videos across five genres by segmenting each video into short clips using a scene-change detection model and shuffling the resulting clips to remove their temporal order. Through objective evaluation and qualitative examples, we demonstrate that Clips2Story can effectively retrieve keyword-relevant clips and compose coherent storyboards based on user-specified keywords. Human evaluation further shows that Clips2Story outperforms a strong baseline in terms of narrative coherence, keyword alignment, and overall realism.

Multimedia.title: LiveFoley: Dynamic Real-Time Video-to-Audio Generation for Immersive Interactive Worlds
Multimedia.summary: Streaming video-to-audio (V2A) generation is essential for immersive interactive applications. However, real-time constraints leave existing streaming V2A methods far behind offline models: (1) visual frontends shrink their receptive fields to cut look-ahead latency, severely degrading audio-visual alignment; (2) causal autoregressive diffusion backends denoise each audio patch in isolation, impairing audio quality. To this end, we present LiveFoley, a streaming causal autoregressive diffusion architecture that addresses both bottlenecks with imperceptible latency. For the visual frontend, we introduce a Trailing Sliding Window that converts non-causal segment-level encoders into streaming modules without retraining. By simply realigning the window, it preserves precise audio-visual alignment, while a configurable hop size reduces the frontend look-ahead well below the human perceptual threshold. Building on this tunable hop size, we propose the Unified Varhop Framework to accommodate scenarios with diverse latency and computation budgets. For the audio backend, we explore widening the denoising window of the local diffusion transformer (LocDiT) head in two temporal directions. History LocDiT adds past context to improve quality at no latency cost and serves as our default. Alternatively, Future-Warmup LocDiT breaks the autoregressive deadlock with an approximate future condition, further improving generation quality at the cost of an acceptable backend look-ahead. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiveFoley matches offline models in temporal alignment and leads streaming systems in generation quality. Project page: https://dalision.github.io/livefoley-page/

Multimedia.title: Chronos: Sequential Identity-Preserving Video Generation by Temporal Anchoring
Multimedia.summary: Identity-preserving video generation aims to synthesize high-quality and visually realistic videos from textual and visual conditions while faithfully maintaining the subject's identity across diverse motions. Prior methods have extensively introduced reference-guided control signals and identity-aware conditioning to improve facial alignment from reference images. However, improving static identity alignment alone creates a fundamental tension between identity fidelity and temporal controllability, which frequently causes identity drift or motion suppression under large pose variations and multi-segment sequential actions. To address this, we propose Chronos, a framework that unifies single-segment facial identity preservation and multi-segment sequential action generation under a common temporal formulation. Specifically, Chronos integrates Semantic Prompt Anchoring to adaptively refine the user prompt, Visual Frame Anchoring to transform conditions into visually grounded keyframe anchors for visual guidance, and Metric-Guided Candidate Routing to select the highest-quality videos from heterogeneous generators via multi-dimensional evaluation. Extensive evaluations demonstrate the superiority of our approach, which achieved first place in both Track 1 and Track 2 of the ACM MM 2026 Identity-Preserving Video Generation Challenge, demonstrating its effectiveness across both facial identity preservation and sequential action generation settings.
Multimedia.comment: Accepted by ACM MM 2026. 1st place in Tracks 1 and 2 of the ACM MM 2026 Identity-Preserving Video Generation Challenge

Computational Geometry.title: Approximating the Euclidean Ball by Polytopes: Surprising Rates in High Dimensions
Computational Geometry.summary:
We provide sharp estimates on the number of vertices needed to approximate the Euclidean unit ball $B_d\subset\mathbb R^d$ with relative symmetric-difference volume error at most $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$. We show that the minimum vertex budget $N_\varepsilon(d)$ satisfies $$\log N_\varepsilon(d)\asymp d\log\left(1+\frac1{\varepsilon\sqrt d}\right).$$ In particular, $\exp(O(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ vertices suffice for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and all sufficiently large $d$. We also prove that achieving a fixed error $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ requires at least $Ω\bigl((\tfrac{1+\varepsilon}{2\sqrt\varepsilon})^{d-1}\bigr)$ facets, an exponential number in $d$. We extend our vertex approximation result to Gaussian symmetric-difference error, and give a positive answer to the question of De, Nadimpalli, and Servedio about subexponential vertex complexity for approximating Euclidean balls.
  We also disprove a Macbeath-type extremality principle for unrestricted vertex approximation. Whereas the ball uniformly maximizes the inscribed approximation error among all convex bodies (Macbeath, 1951), we show that approximating the hypercube $[-1,1]^d$ to relative error $\varepsilon$, with $δ:=1-\varepsilon$, requires $N\ge\fracδ{2}\exp(Ω(δ^2d/\log^2(2/δ)))$ vertices whenever $d\ge16\log(2/δ)$. Thus, when $d$ is large, the cube is harder to approximate than the ball in this sense.
  Finally, we determine the sharp dimensional order of the classical Laguerre-Delone triangulation number, showing that $\mathrm{ldel}_{d-1}=Θ(d^{-1/2})$ as $d\to\infty$. This improves both the upper bound of Ludwig, Schütt, and Werner and the lower bound of Böröczky by a factor of order $\sqrt d$. By classical asymptotic approximation theorems (Ludwig, 1999), this improvement applies to every convex body in $\mathbb R^d$ with $C^2$ boundary and positive Gaussian curvature.
Computational Geometry.comment: 71 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. v2: exposition and references revised for a broader audience

Computational Geometry.title: Counterexamples to the Happy Edge Conjecture in Plane Spanning Trees
Computational Geometry.summary:
We study the problem of reconfiguring plane, straight-line spanning trees on point sets in the plane. A flip is a reconfiguration step in which one edge of a tree is replaced with another, yielding again a plane spanning tree. For a given point set $P$, the flip graph has a vertex for each plane spanning tree on $P$, and an edge between any two trees that differ by a single flip.
  The folklore happy edge conjecture suggests that any edge shared by both the initial and the target tree (a happy edge) is never flipped in a shortest flip sequence. This conjecture was computationally verified for up to 10 points in convex position.
  In this paper, we disprove this conjecture both on general point sets and on point sets in convex position by providing two counterexamples on $16$ and $30$ points, respectively. The counterexample for point sets in general position also holds for compatible flips, while the happy edge property holds for compatible flips in convex point sets as shown by Aichholzer, Dorfer, and Vogtenhuber [GD 2025].

Computational Geometry.title: A Linear Lower Bound for Convex Body Chasing in Every Norm
Computational Geometry.summary: We establish an $Ω(d)$ lower bound on the competitive ratio of convex body chasing in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with movement costs measured in any norm. Previously, the best known lower bound valid across all norms was $Ω(d^{1/6})$, established by Papazov (2023); stronger lower bounds were known for $\ell_p$ norms, where Bubeck, Klartag, Lee, Li, and Sellke (2019) had established a lower bound of $Ω(\max\{\sqrt{d}, d^{1-1/p}\})$. In particular, a linear lower bound was known only for the $\ell_\infty$ norm, realized by the standard construction of chasing faces of a hypercube. Our lower bound strictly improves on the prior universal and $\ell_p$ lower bounds for $p < \infty$ and shows that the functional Steiner point algorithm of Sellke (2023) - which has competitive ratio $O(d)$ - is asymptotically optimal for every norm. Our approach is based on the recursive construction of Bubeck, Coester, and Rabani (2023) for metrical service systems, which gives a lower bound of $Ω(r^2)$ for requests of size $O(r)$. We show that requests in their construction, each comprising a set of discrete points in a graph metric, can be mapped to the vertices of convex requests in a $(2r+1)$-dimensional $\ell_p$ vector space while approximately preserving movement costs up to a factor of $O(r)$; the general result then follows via Milman's (1985) quotient-of-a-subspace theorem.
Computational Geometry.comment: Updates the previous version to extend the lower bound to all norms

Computational Geometry.title: A Two-Count Baseline for Change Detection on Dynamic Networks
Computational Geometry.summary: Change-point detectors for dynamic networks aim to find changes in how a network is connected. They are evaluated on real networks with labelled events, but many of these events also change how active the network is: how many vertices take part and how many edges are present. A detector can therefore score well by responding to activity alone, without detecting any change in structure. We test whether detectors from the literature beat a simple baseline that tracks only the number of active vertices and the number of edges in each snapshot, a baseline that we motivate with a standard statistical test for a change in activity. On ten datasets, four of them from the papers of published detectors, none of thirteen detectors ranks the labelled events significantly better than the baseline when the results are pooled (AUC $0.75$, or $0.73$ with scales taken from early snapshots only, against $0.66$ for the best detector). The baseline is best on only two datasets, however, and on the four datasets with the most events three detectors that track individual vertices score higher. When we rewire networks while keeping the degree of every vertex fixed, most detectors that ignore vertex identities barely respond, but several that track individual vertices do. New detectors should be compared with this baseline and tested at fixed degree.

Computational Geometry.title: Faster Planar Diameter using Pseudoline Envelopes
Computational Geometry.summary:
We give an improved algorithm for weighted directed planar diameter that runs in $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ time. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})$ time algorithm for weighted directed planar diameter of Gawrychowski, Kaplan, Mozes, Sharir, and Weimann [SIAM J. Comput. 2021] and the recent $\widetilde{O}(n^{8/5})$ time algorithm for unweighted undirected planar diameter of Fredslund-Hansen, Mozes, and Weimann [SOSA 2027].
  The main new result is an improved data structure for computing the farthest vertex when given feasible planar distances to the vertices on the outer face. The critical insight is the fact that normalized distances to the vertices of a face behave like pseudolines, for which we can leverage range searching and upper envelope data structures. Using the farthest vertex data structure, we are able to compute all vertex eccentricities and diameter in $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$.

Computational Geometry.title: Representation-Aware Closed-Surface Parameterization: Exact Sensitivity Analysis and Pole-Aware Planar Preconditioning
Computational Geometry.summary: Surface parameterization is a fundamental task in geometry processing and shape analysis. For topologically closed surfaces, it is common to parameterize them onto a standardized closed domain in $\mathbb{R}^3$, with a prime example being a unit sphere for genus-0 closed surfaces. Many mapping methods use planar projections and perform computations on the plane rather than directly on the 3D surface. However, perturbations introduced before projection or geometric evolution propagate through the computation and may affect map quality, convergence, stopping behavior, and geometric validity. In this work, we formulate representation sensitivity as a branchwise input--output problem, separating smooth propagation through active Jacobians from changes in anchors, stopping rules, and fallback events. Under consistent piecewise-linear assembly, the unmodified south-pole Beltrami correction in the FLASH method for spherical conformal parameterization reduces exactly to source-mesh harmonic extension. On a fixed-anchor branch, the corrected map factors into chart transition, harmonic propagation, and inverse stereographic projection, yielding an explicit sensitivity Jacobian and a finite-triangle conditioning bound. Separately, we introduce a bounded five-parameter affine preconditioner over planar scale, translation, and anisotropy and evaluate candidates on the corrected spherical map. Across 30 genus-0 surfaces, it reduces median polar upper-tail log-condition and chord-angle distortion by $10.17\%$ and $10.97\%$, respectively, with both measures improving on every mesh. We also apply the framework to other spherical mapping methods including the conformalized mean-curvature flow and spherical density-equalizing maps. Altogether, our work highlights the importance of representation selection as a structural and practical component of spherical parameterization and downstream computation.

Computational Geometry.title: The Stretch Factor of Planar Delaunay Triangulations Is Nearly Determined
Computational Geometry.summary: The Delaunay triangulation is a classical geometric structure on a finite set of points in the plane. Its stretch factor is the largest ratio of the shortest-path distance along its edges to the Euclidean distance between the same two points. Determining the worst-case stretch factor of planar Delaunay triangulations is a long-standing open problem. We prove a uniform upper bound of 1.5949, improving the previous bound of 1.998 and narrowing the gap to the best known lower bound of 1.5932 from 0.4048 to less than 0.0017, nearly pinpointing the worst-case stretch factor. A central difficulty is that the line segment between two points may cross arbitrarily many triangles. Our progress accounting framework addresses this by converting the global bound into a family of local inequalities, each involving only a fixed number of real parameters regardless of the number of triangles crossed. Two further geometric lemmas make computer-assisted verification tractable: the pencil lemma decomposes each local transition into two geometrically independent stages, reducing verification over infinitely many possible next disks to a single differential condition; and the corner lemmas handle degenerate boundary cases where direct verification would fail. With these reductions, the proof ends with a finite verification of an explicit potential in exact rational arithmetic and outward-rounded interval arithmetic. Numerous geometric network constructions use the Delaunay stretch factor as a black box, so the tighter bound directly improves stretch-factor guarantees for a range of downstream applications, including bounded-degree plane spanners and low-weight spanners.
Computational Geometry.comment: 67 pages, 14 figures, 8 tables. Substantially revised: the upper bound is improved from 1.65 to 1.5949, and the title has changed. Verification data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23835635

Computational Geometry.title: A $(3+ε)$-Approximation for Fair $k$-Means and a Matching Lower Bound
Computational Geometry.summary: Fair clustering aims to prevent algorithmic bias against protected groups. We study Euclidean fair $k$-means, in which the proportion of each protected group in every cluster lies between prescribed lower and upper bounds. Because these constraints violate the nearest-center assignment property, center selection is coupled with point assignment. We introduce the drift-regularized relaxation, a new convex relaxation solved by a modified Frank-Wolfe method with linear-programming iterations, whose optimality condition controls the cost of converting its solution into $k$ fair clusters. Combined with any $ρ$-approximation algorithm for weighted $k$-means, the relaxation yields an exactly fair fractional solution of cost at most $2ρ+1+ε$ times the fractional optimum, improving the previous ratio $1+4ρ+ε$. In fixed dimension, this improves the best known ratio from $5+O(ε)$ to $3+O(ε)$. The fractional solution can be rounded to an integral one without changing the centers or increasing the cost, at a bounded additive violation of the fairness bounds. We also show that a $(3-δ)$-approximation is NP-hard for every fixed $δ>0$, even on the line with fractional assignments, so $3$ is the exact approximation threshold for fractional fair $k$-means in fixed dimension. The same guarantees hold for $k$-sparse Wasserstein barycenters, a special case of fractional fair $k$-means. More generally, they hold whenever every cluster must satisfy given homogeneous linear inequalities in the fractions of its points, such as a bound on the ratio between two groups or on the average of a numerical attribute in every cluster.

Computational Geometry.title: Constant-Factor Approximation for Capacitated Clustering in Low Dimension with $(1+ε)k$ Centers
Computational Geometry.summary:
In many applications of $k$-median and $k$-means, including load balancing and redistricting, each center can serve only a bounded number of clients. This leads to capacitated clustering, in which a client may be forced to use a distant center because all nearby ones are full. This loss of locality defeats the techniques behind approximation schemes, and no constant-factor approximation is known in general metrics even for capacitated $k$-median. A long line of work therefore opens $K=k+\lfloorεk\rfloor$ centers for a fixed $ε\in(0,1]$, while respecting the capacities exactly.
  We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for uniform soft capacities in low dimension, that is, when the clients or the center locations have bounded doubling dimension. With $K$ centers, its ratio is $3-2ε$ for $k$-median and $9-8ε$ for $k$-means, or $5-4ε$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Apart from $k$-median in the plane, these are the first polynomial-time ratios bounded by a constant independent of $ε$; previously, the best ratio was $O(ε^{-2}\log(1/ε))$, even for $k$-median. We also obtain ratios that stay bounded as $ε\to0$ for non-uniform and hard capacities in low dimension, and ratios polylogarithmic in $1/ε$ in general metrics.
  Our approach starts from a simple structural observation: a near-optimal uncapacitated solution can be split into fewer than $2k$ capacity-respecting blocks, so $2k$ centers already suffice, one per block. Our main tool, the rescue lemma, shows that once every block that sends clients to a center of the optimal solution is rescued (given a private center), that center can be closed, so each extra center effectively rescues about two blocks. This lets $\lfloorεk\rfloor$ extra centers rescue nearly an $ε$-fraction of the blocks, yielding the linear dependence on $ε$ in our ratios.

Computational Geometry.title: Geometric Bin Packing Beyond Convexity: Approximation Schemes without Augmentation
Computational Geometry.summary:
We study the geometric bin packing problem for simple polygonal regions, i.e., non-degenerate, connected, rational regions, in the minimum number of unit-square bins, allowing only translations. We even consider packing general non-convex objects, possibly with holes, where we can then pack smaller objects. Previous schemes cover squares (MOR'06), circles and other $L_p$-balls (Algorithmica'16), sufficiently skewed rectangles (Algorithmica'23), and convex fat objects with a constant number of distinct shapes under resource augmentation (arXiv'24, WAOA'23). The result for circles and other $L_p$-balls needs bin augmentation to obtain rational packing realizations. For restricted classes of $L$-shaped polygons, Gerlach et al. (SoCG'26) give constant worst-case guarantees, while for general non-convex objects, bounding-box reductions give just approximation factors that depend on fatness.
  Against this background, we present a general framework that provides asymptotic polynomial-time approximation schemes (APTAS) for bin packing of any fixed class of simple polygonal regions satisfying just two assumptions. First, covering any object by the grid cells intersecting its interior in any sufficiently fine square grid, relative to the object's bounding box, increases its area by at most a small fraction. Second, the class can be partitioned into a constant number of sequences such that each object in a sequence can be translated to fit inside every preceding object. In particular, certain classes of star-shaped polygons and more general polygonal regions, including some with simple holes, satisfy both assumptions. In addition, our framework does not require a bound on the objects' boundary complexity. We emphasize that our results require no bin augmentation whatsoever and yield explicit, exact rational packings of polynomial encoding length for all input objects.

Computational Geometry.title: Scalable Exact Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering via Sparse Geographic Distance Graphs
Computational Geometry.summary: Exact hierarchical agglomerative clustering (HAC) of large spatial datasets is limited in practice by the $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ time and memory required for the full pairwise distance matrix. We present GSHAC (Geographically Sparse Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering), a system that makes exact HAC feasible at scales of millions of geographic features on a commodity workstation. GSHAC replaces the distance matrix with a sparse geographic distance graph containing only pairs within a user-specified geodesic bound $h_{\max}$, constructed in $\mathcal{O}(n \cdot k)$ time via spatial indexing, where $k$ is the mean number of neighbors within $h_{\max}$. Connected components of this graph define independent subproblems, and we prove that the resulting assignments are exact for all standard linkage methods at any cut height $h \le h_{\max}$. For single linkage, an MST-based path keeps memory at $\mathcal{O}(n_k + m_k)$ per component. Applied to a global mining inventory ($n = 261{,}073$), the system completes in 12 s (109 MiB peak HAC memory) versus $\approx 545$ GiB for the dense baseline. On a 2-million-point GeoNames sample, all tested thresholds completed in under 3 minutes with peak memory under 3 GiB. We provide a scikit-learn-compatible implementation for direct integration into GIS workflows.

Computational Geometry.title: Tight Coreset Bounds for $(k,z)$-Clustering in Euclidean and Doubling Metrics
Computational Geometry.summary:
We determine the optimal worst-case size of strong coresets for $(k,z)$-clustering in Euclidean spaces and doubling metrics, up to polylogarithmic factors.
